docs.text:
Short recordings of narratty's features, each with the spec that made it. The specs are in examples/; build one with narratty build <spec>.

Example Shows Select with Markdown input A docs page turned into its own video markdown entry Voices and engines Kokoro and Piper voices, English and German tts.provider, tts.voice Pronunciation Terms spelled as in the code, spoken correctly tts.lexicon Terminal look Theme, font, prompt, typing speed terminal Editor layout Explorer, preview and shell in one tmux window terminal.layout: editor Subtitles and drafts Burned-in subtitles; a fast preview without TTS subtitles, --draft Asciicast player Selectable terminal text with a narration track --format cast Web pages The project's GitHub page, captured and scrolled browser Overlays Chapter titles, file names, notes over the video overlay, overlay_styles Dev container A build recorded in the project's dev container environment.compose End card "Created with narratty" card with logo, link and QR code end_card, --no-end-card

All recordings except the end card example are built with --no-end-card. examples/render-docs.sh rebuilds them (--only browser just the specs whose path contains browser) and stores a fingerprint of each spec next to it; a unit test fails when a spec changed since its videos were rendered. Videos made from Markdown, like the one on Markdown input, are rendered in CI before each docs deploy instead, so they always match their page (examples/render-ci-videos.sh).

docs.title: Web pages
docs.text:
A browser action shows a web page or a local HTML file in the video. Headless Chromium (in the narratty image) captures it once and scrolls it. See Browser views.

# A web page in the video: the project's GitHub page, captured by Chromium.
version: 1
meta:
  title: Show a web page
terminal:
  width: 1280
  height: 720
  font_size: 20
sandbox:
  network: full       # the page is loaded from GitHub
scenes:
  - id: clone
    narration: Everything starts on the project's GitHub page.
    actions:
      - type_command: git clone https://github.com/ditschi/narratty
      - hold: 300ms
  - id: page
    narration: >-
      This is the page you should see. The readme explains what narratty does, and
      further down you find the quick start.
    actions:
      - browser: {url: "https://github.com/ditschi/narratty", scroll: 1400, load_ms: 15s}
  - id: back
    narration: Back in the terminal, copy the clone command and press Enter.
    actions:
      - key: Enter
      - hold: 500ms
  • scroll: auto scrolls to the end of the page (at most 4 screens).
  • Local files (site/index.html) need no network.
  • To browse inside the terminal instead, run a text browser such as w3m or lynx, or glow for Markdown. They are not in the image; add them with environment.packages.

docs.title: Asciicast player
docs.text:
--format cast writes an asciicast, the narration as MP3 and an HTML page that plays both. The text stays selectable, and the audio drives the player, so seeking stays in sync.

narratty build examples/cast/cast.narratty.yaml --format cast   # cast.cast, cast.mp3, cast.html

terminal: {width: 960, height: 540, font_size: 20}
scenes:
  - id: intro
    narration: >-
      This is not a video. It is an asciicast with a narration track, so you can
      select and copy the text.
    actions:
      - run: ls -1
  - id: size
    narration: The recording itself is only a few kilobytes.
    actions:
      - run: echo "Hello from an asciicast"

See Asciicast with narration to embed the .cast and .mp3 in your own page.

docs.title: Editor layout
docs.text:
terminal.layout: editor: yazi as explorer and preview on top, a shell below, in one tmux window. focus and reveal move between the panes, diff shows what the demo changed. See Editor layout for the details.

terminal:
  layout: editor
scenes:
  - id: explore
    narration: Switch to the explorer and open the source folder.
    pause_ms: 600ms
    actions:
      - focus: explorer
      - key: Right
      - key: Right
      - key: Down
  - id: run
    narration: Back in the terminal, run the program.
    actions:
      - focus: terminal
      - run: PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m greet Ada Grace
      - wait: "Hello, Grace!"
  - id: diff
    narration: Finally, the diff shows everything this demo changed.
    actions:
      - diff

narratty build examples/editor-layout/editor.narratty.yaml

docs.title: End card
docs.text:
Every video ends with a 4 s card: the logo, "Created with narratty", a link to these docs and a QR code of the link.

To leave it out:

Scope Setting One build narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --no-end-card One spec end_card: false All your builds [end_card] enabled = false in ~/.config/narratty/config.toml

end_card.duration_ms sets the length, end_card.qr: false drops the QR code. See end_card.

docs.title: Pronunciation
docs.text:
Narration keeps the real spelling of terms (k8s, kubectx), so it stays correct and searchable. The lexicon tells the engine how to say them. See Pronunciation.

With the lexicon:

Without it ("k eight z", "cube ect x"):

tts:
  lexicon:
    k8s: kubernetes
    kubectx: cube C T X
    ttyd: T T Y D
terminal: {width: 960, height: 540, font_size: 20}
scenes:
  - id: lexicon
    narration: >-
      Deploy to k8s with kubectl, switch clusters with kubectx, and share the
      terminal with ttyd.
    actions:
      - run: "grep -m1 -A4 tts: lexicon.narratty.yaml"

kubectl needs no entry: it is in the built-in lexicon. Put entries shared by several specs in narratty.lexicon.toml in the repository or ~/.config/narratty/lexicon.toml.

lexicon check lists words that may need an entry, lexicon show the merged entries and where each comes from:

$ narratty lexicon check examples/lexicon/lexicon.narratty.yaml
every unusual word has a lexicon entry
$ narratty lexicon show examples/lexicon/lexicon.narratty.yaml

docs.title: Subtitles
docs.text:
Subtitles come from the narration, one cue per sentence. This spec burns them in:

subtitles: burn
terminal: {width: 960, height: 540, font_size: 20}
scenes:
  - id: intro
    narration: >-
      Subtitles come from the narration. Each sentence becomes one cue, and a long
      sentence is split so that it fits in two lines.
    actions:
      - run: "grep -m1 subtitles subtitles.narratty.yaml"
  - id: modes
    narration: Burned in, as here, or as files, or as a track that players can switch.
    actions:
      - run: 'echo "subtitles: none | files | track | burn"'
subtitles / --subtitles Result files .srt and .vtt beside the video track Soft track in the mp4, switchable in the player burn Drawn into the picture

docs.title: Draft
docs.text:
--draft previews actions and timing without TTS: estimated narration lengths, half size, 10 fps, narration burned in as subtitles. The same spec as a draft:

narratty build examples/subtitles/subtitles.narratty.yaml --draft   # subtitles.draft.mp4

See Building a video for details.

docs.title: Terminal look
docs.text:
The terminal block sets the video size, font size, VHS theme, prompt and typing speed. See terminal.

terminal:
  width: 960
  height: 540
  font_size: 24
  theme: Catppuccin Mocha
  prompt: "❯ "
  typing_speed_ms: 70
scenes:
  - id: look
    narration: >-
      The terminal block sets the size, font, theme, prompt and typing speed. Any
      VHS theme works.
    actions:
      - run: "grep -m1 -A6 terminal: terminal-look.narratty.yaml"
  • shell: zsh (or fish, sh) records another shell.
  • A scene's own typing_speed_ms overrides the global one.

docs.title: Voices and engines
docs.text:
Two local engines: Kokoro (default, natural) and Piper (more languages, including German). Pick them in the spec's tts block; narratty voices lists the curated voices. See Voices and audio cache.

Kokoro af_heartKokoro am_michaelKokoro bf_emmaPiper lessacPiper thorsten (German)

Default; the spec needs no tts block for it.

tts:
  provider: kokoro
  voice: af_heart


tts:
  provider: kokoro
  voice: am_michael


tts:
  provider: kokoro
  voice: bf_emma


tts:
  provider: piper
  voice: en_US-lessac-medium


tts:
  provider: piper
  voice: de_DE-thorsten-medium
  • With only provider, the voice is that provider's first curated voice.
  • Speed: kokoro.speed (1.0 = normal) or piper.length_scale (larger is slower).
  • Voices download on first use; narratty voices pull <id> fetches one ahead.
narratty build examples/voices/kokoro-bf_emma.narratty.yaml

docs.title: Building a video
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml            # writes demo.mp4 next to the spec
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml -o out/tour.mp4 --work-dir out/work

build runs the whole pipeline:

  1. Narration. Each narrated scene's text is synthesized, or taken from the audio cache.
  2. Timeline. Each scene lasts as long as its actions, or as long as its narration plus timing.narration_buffer_ms, whichever is longer.
  3. Tape. A VHS tape types your commands and pauses to fill each scene.
  4. Recording. VHS records a silent video, running the shell in workspace.source.
  5. Mix. Every clip is placed at the start of its scene as recorded, in one narration track, which is muxed onto the video as AAC.
  6. Check. The result must contain video and audio, and no narration may run past the end of its scene by more than --max-drift of its length (10% by default). Otherwise the build exits with code 6.

After the last scene and the tail comes the end card (4 s by default; see end_card); --no-end-card leaves it out.

With --work-dir the tape, the silent video and the narration track are kept for inspection.

docs.title: Scene Recording Cache
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --scene-cache
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --scene-cache --refresh-scene-cache
narratty cache info
narratty cache prune --scenes --older-than 30d

The opt-in scene cache reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the silent recording. It replays those scenes hidden in the same shell to restore their state, records the remaining scenes and joins the video. The last visible scene is always recorded again. Commands and waits in reused scenes still run, so the cache saves recording work, not the time spent running commands or waiting. A changed scene invalidates it and all following scenes. Narration can change without invalidating the footage when its duration and the rest of the scene timing stay the same. The cache stores only the recordings VHS made, never a joined video, so reused scenes are re-encoded once per build and do not lose quality over repeated builds.

The cache fingerprints the workspace files, scene inputs, timeline, narratty's own code, the recording tools (VHS and its version, ttyd, ffmpeg, the shells, the browser VHS launches), the installed fonts, the container image and the environment variables that change terminal output (TERM, COLORTERM, LANG, LANGUAGE, LC_*, TZ, SHELL, PATH, HOME, NO_COLOR and the spec's env_passthrough). In a git repository, files git ignores (such as .venv or node_modules) count by size and modification time instead of their contents; other files count by contents. The git history itself does not count. The spec and generated output files are excluded from the workspace fingerprint. It cannot track every external dependency: network responses, time, files outside the workspace, symlink targets, other environment variables, running services and commands that read the excluded files can change the result. Replayed commands may also produce different state than the cached footage shows. Use --refresh-scene-cache with --scene-cache to force a fresh recording after such a change, and for final builds where reproducibility matters.

Caching currently requires at least two visible scenes and falls back to a normal recording with drafts, fast pauses, timelapses, overlays, browser views, slides or a project environment. It applies only to MP4 builds. Natively it also needs --workspace-mode rw (or ro): a native snapshot gets a new directory each build, which shows in prompts and output. In a container the snapshot is always at /work, so snapshots are cached there. Sandboxed scene-cache builds use the stable container hostname narratty.

Every build that records new scenes adds a recording to the cache, so it grows with use. narratty cache info shows its size; narratty cache prune --scenes --older-than 30d removes entries not used for that long, the recordings only they referenced and files left by interrupted builds, and cache prune --scenes --all removes all scene recordings without touching the audio cache. If the cache cannot be written (a full disk, a read-only cache directory) the build still succeeds and logs scene cache not updated.

docs.title: Subtitles
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --subtitles files   # demo.mp4, demo.srt, demo.vtt

Subtitles come from the narration: each clip becomes one cue per sentence, and long sentences are split so a cue fits in two lines. Cues show the text as written in the spec. Set the mode with subtitles or --subtitles:

Mode Result none No subtitles (default) files .srt and .vtt beside the video track A soft subtitle track in the mp4; players can switch it on and off burn Drawn into the picture; re-encodes the video

With --format cast, every mode except none writes the .srt and .vtt beside the page.

docs.title: Draft
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --draft      # writes demo.draft.mp4

A draft checks actions and timing without waiting for TTS:

  • narration lengths are estimated from the text (about 14 characters per second, scaled by the voice speed); no voice is loaded or downloaded;
  • VHS captures 10 frames per second instead of 30, and the video is encoded at half size; the terminal itself keeps its size, so output and wait behave as in the real build;
  • long pauses are fast; one that does not end on a still screen is logged, not an error;
  • the video is silent and the narration is burned in as subtitles, so you see where each line would be spoken (--subtitles picks another mode).

narratty plan SPEC --draft prints the estimated timeline. --draft only applies to mp4 output.

docs.title: Fast pauses
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --fast

Most of a narrated video is pauses: the screen holds still while the voice talks. VHS records in real time, so a 10 s pause costs 10 s of recording. With --fast, a visible pause longer than 1 s is recorded for 1 s, and its last frame is repeated for the rest. The video is as long as without --fast; the cursor does not blink.

That is only right when the screen is still at the end of that second, so narratty checks the recording and fails, naming the scene, when

  • the screen changed in the last half second, or
  • a command the scene started is still running (it might print later). Interactive programs (editors, pagers, tmux) do not count; they wait for keys.

For a command that runs longer, add a wait for its last output before the pause, or set fast: false on the scene. The running-command check reads /proc, so it only works on Linux (natively or in the container). In the editor layout it only sees tmux, so there only the screen is checked. Pauses in timelapse scenes are recorded in full; those scenes are sped up anyway.

A scene's fast overrides the command line: fast: false records its pauses in full even with --fast, fast: true fills them even without it.

scenes:
  - id: build
    fast: false        # output may still arrive during the pause
    actions:
      - run: make

With --format cast, --fast skips the rest of a pause once there has been no output for half a second and no command is running. The cast's timestamps are the same as without it.

docs.title: Asciicast with narration
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --format cast   # demo.cast, demo.mp3, demo.html

Instead of a video, this writes an asciicast (.cast), the narration as MP3, and an HTML page that plays both with asciinema-player. The player uses the audio as its clock, so pausing and seeking stay in sync. Terminal text stays selectable, and the cast is a few kilobytes.

  • The page is self-contained: cast and audio are embedded, so it works opened from disk or on any static host. The player itself loads from jsDelivr.
  • -o names the page; the .cast and .mp3 go beside it.
  • Recording: VHS cannot write asciicasts, so narratty runs the scenes itself in a pseudo-terminal of the same size and shell. Each clip is placed at its scene's recorded start, so there is no drift check.
  • Size: columns and rows follow terminal.width, height and font_size. The theme applies when asciinema-player has one of the same name (Dracula, Monokai, Nord, Solarized, Tango, …).
  • Overlays are drawn over the player as HTML boxes and follow its clock. The .cast itself has none: asciicast has no way to store them. The same goes for browser views, which the page shows as images over the player.
  • wait matches the text printed since the last clear, not a rendered screen; full-screen programs such as vim are not modelled.

To embed the recording in your own page, use the .cast and .mp3:

AsciinemaPlayer.create("demo.cast", element, { audioUrl: "demo.mp3" });

Seeking needs a server that supports range requests, as most static hosts do.

docs.title: Looking before rendering
docs.text: Command Shows narratty plan SPEC Each scene's start, action time, narration length and the total, with measured command durations narratty plan SPEC --draft The same with estimated narration lengths, without TTS narratty tape SPEC The generated VHS tape narratty render SPEC Records only the silent video (demo.silent.mp4)

docs.title: How sync works
docs.text:
Narration starts when its scene starts, so the voice talks while the command is typed. Set narration_start: after_actions on a scene to speak only after its actions. The pause that fills a scene goes after its actions; at a hold: auto the scene waits until the narration and timing.narration_buffer_ms are done, so what follows starts after the voice has finished (before 0.7 it only waited for what the actions after it did not fill).

The recording notes where each scene really started, and for after_actions where its actions really ended. Each clip is placed there, so a command that takes longer than planned moves only its own scene's narration; later scenes stay in sync, and hold: auto (explain, then run) and after_actions (run, then explain) keep their order. Subtitles follow the clips; overlays, headings, slides, table rows and Mermaid focus follow the moments they were recorded at.

A longer scene only adds a pause, so the drift check does not compare the video's length with the plan. It fails when a narration runs into the next scene, and names the scene and why, e.g. intro (0.80s over: scene recorded 0.80s shorter than planned). Shorter narration overruns are logged as warnings. The CLI still prints the video's and the plan's length.

When VHS writes no scene markers, the planned clip positions are stretched to the video's length instead.

docs.title: Dropped frames
docs.text: VHS takes frames in real time. On a busy machine it misses some, and the video comes out shorter than the time it recorded, so everything on screen happens too early. narratty compares the two right after recording. When the video is more than 3% (and at least half a second) short, it logs a warning naming both lengths and stretches the recording back to real time, repeating frames, before anything is placed on it. Typing then looks a little less smooth, but the narration matches. Build on a quieter machine for the best picture.

docs.title: Measured command durations
docs.text:
The plan counts a run as its typing plus timing.run_hold_ms; it cannot know that make takes twelve seconds. narratty check runs every command anyway and notes how long each took, from Enter until the shell was back:

$ narratty check demo.narratty.yaml
recorded how long 6 commands took; plans now wait for the slow ones: build (12.3s)

plan, tape and build then pause after such a command until it is done (plus 0.3 s), so its output is on screen before the scene goes on, the narration's fill shrinks accordingly, and plan shows realistic lengths. They log the commands they wait for, and plan lists the scenes that use measurements.

  • Measurements are kept in the cache directory (command-durations.json), keyed by the spec's title, the shell, the layout, the scene and the command. Changing a command forgets its measurement; run check again to update them.
  • A command stopped with a control key (C-c) or still running at the end is not measured. A wait needs no measurement: it blocks until the output is there.
  • With job control off (set +m), commands are only measured on Linux.
  • timing.measured_durations: false plans with run_hold_ms only, e.g. for builds that must not depend on an earlier check.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• wait matches the whole screen, including the command you just typed. Wait for text that only the command's output contains, e.g. wait: {screen: "Build succeeded"} rather than a word that also appears in the command.
  • Slow commands make their scene longer than planned, but only that scene. Run narratty check first, so the plan waits for them, or move the slow part into a hidden scene.
  • A video shorter than planned means VHS dropped frames, usually because the machine was busy. narratty stretches the recording back to real time and warns; if the drift check still fails, the error shows the load average. Build again when the machine is idle.
  • Hidden scenes run without being recorded and clear the screen afterwards, which makes them good for setup such as cd, exporting variables or warming caches.
  • The workspace is a throwaway snapshot by default, so demos can build and write files without touching your checkout; see workspace modes.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
SPEC is a .narratty.yaml file or, since 0.6, a Markdown doc built on its own with the spec it implies (see Building a doc on its own).

Command Does narratty init [FILE] [--force] Write a commented starter spec (default demo.narratty.yaml) narratty init --markdown DOC [FILE] Write a spec that makes the video from DOC (default <doc>.narratty.yaml) (since 0.6) narratty validate SPEC Check a spec; report every problem, and hints for redundant lines, with line and column narratty schema Print the spec's JSON Schema narratty compile SPEC [-o FILE] Print the spec with its Markdown entries expanded (since 0.5) narratty compile SPEC --fingerprint Print a hash of what the video shows and says, to notice when a committed video is outdated (since 0.5) narratty voices [--provider P] [--installed] List curated and installed voices narratty voices pull VOICE Download a voice (and the Kokoro model) narratty tts SPEC [--offline] Synthesize all narration clips and print their lengths narratty lexicon show SPEC List the pronunciation lexicon entries and where each comes from narratty lexicon check SPEC List narration words that look hard to pronounce and have no entry narratty cache info / prune [--older-than 30d] [--all] [--scenes] Inspect caches or prune the audio cache (or, with --scenes, the scene recording cache, including leftovers of interrupted builds) narratty plan SPEC [--draft] Print the timeline and total length narratty plan SPEC --sources List where each scene comes from (Markdown file and line) and what was left out (since 0.5) narratty tape SPEC [-o VIDEO] Print the VHS tape narratty render SPEC [-o VIDEO] Record the silent video narratty build SPEC [-o VIDEO] [--work-dir DIR] [--max-drift 0.10] Build the narrated video narratty build SPEC --subtitles MODE Add subtitles: none, files, track or burn narratty build SPEC --draft Build a fast draft (demo.draft.mp4) narratty build SPEC --fast Fill long pauses with still frames instead of recording them (fast pauses) narratty build SPEC --scene-cache [--refresh-scene-cache] Reuse unchanged recordings, or force a fresh recording (scene cache) narratty build SPEC --ignore-exit Don't check exit codes, except where the spec sets expect_exit (exit codes) narratty build SPEC --format cast [-o PAGE] Build an asciicast with narration narratty check SPEC Run the commands without recording; check their exit codes and output (since 0.6), and record how long they take for later plans (since 0.7) narratty env shell SPEC Open a shell in the spec's project environment narratty env build SPEC [--rebuild-env] Build the environment's image and print its tag narratty env up SPEC Start the environment and keep it; build, render and env shell reuse it narratty env down SPEC Remove what env up started

plan, tape, render and build take --end-card / --no-end-card to override end_card. build, render and check also take --workspace-mode, --keep-workspace, --allow-dirty, --network, --allow-host and --yes; see Sandboxed runs. They take --env-image, --no-env, --keep-env and --rebuild-env for project environments. Every command that runs the pipeline takes --runtime and --image.

Command Does narratty doctor [--runtime R] Check the tools the selected runtime needs narratty --version Print the version narratty --install-completion Install shell completion

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 ok 1 unexpected error 2 usage error 3 spec validation error 4 missing dependency (tool, voice or container runtime) 5 render or mux failure 6 sync verification failure 7 a recorded command exited contrary to its expect_exit 8 a command printed other output than its expect_output (narratty check)

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Path Holds ~/.config/narratty/config.toml Your defaults and limits (below) ~/.config/narratty/lexicon.toml Your pronunciation entries ~/.config/narratty/approvals.json Sandbox permissions you approved, per spec ~/.local/share/narratty/ Downloaded voices and models ~/.cache/narratty/ Audio cache, workspace snapshots, build caches

Paths follow the platform's conventions (on macOS under ~/Library).

docs.title: config.toml
docs.text:
[end_card]
enabled = false                    # no closing card unless a spec or flag asks for it

[sandbox]
max_network = "allowlist"          # none | allowlist | full
allow_env = ["LM_LICENSE_FILE"]    # env_passthrough names a spec may use
allow_mounts = true
allow_ssh_agent = false
allow_docker = false               # no spec gets your Docker/Podman engine
allow_environment = ["image", "compose", "container"]
allow_packages = true              # environment.packages and setup

Every key is optional. A command-line flag beats the spec, and the spec beats this file. [sandbox] is a cap: a spec asking for more fails. See Sandboxed runs.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Effect NARRATTY_RUNTIME auto, native, docker or podman (same as --runtime) NARRATTY_IMAGE Container image (same as --image) NARRATTY_OFFLINE 1: never download voices (same as --offline) NARRATTY_YES 1: approve sandbox permissions without asking (same as --yes) NARRATTY_CONFIG_DIR Directory of config.toml and approvals.json NARRATTY_DATA_DIR Directory for voices and models NARRATTY_CACHE_DIR Directory for caches NARRATTY_AGENT_DIR Local narratty-agent builds (<dir>/<arch>/narratty-agent) instead of the image's NO_COLOR Plain output

docs.title: Sandboxed runs
docs.text:
With Docker or Podman installed, build, render, check, tts, plan and tape run inside the narratty image by default (--runtime auto); plan --draft only estimates and runs on the host. The image contains VHS, ttyd, Chromium, Mermaid, Font Awesome icons, emoji and terminal fonts, ffmpeg, Kokoro, Piper, git, tree, the Docker CLI (with Compose and Buildx) and the demo toolkit (bat, delta, eza, fd, ripgrep, jq, micro, yazi, tmux, zsh). You only need narratty itself and a container runtime on the host.

To run the demo shell in your project's own image instead, see Project environments.

narratty build demo.narratty.yaml                    # container if available
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --runtime native   # tools from your PATH
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --runtime podman

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Image Contents ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty:<version> Kokoro with af_heart, Piper with en_US-lessac-medium ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit:<version> Only the demo toolkit, to copy into other images

narratty picks the tag matching its own version (edge for development builds). Override the image with --image or NARRATTY_IMAGE. Up to 0.1, Kokoro needed a separate -kokoro image; from 0.2 on, the one image has both engines.

The image is about 2 GB. When it is not there yet, narratty says pulling <image> (this can take a while)… and shows the engine's progress on stderr before it starts the first container. A failed pull (pull access denied, no network) stops with the engine's message and what to do: point NARRATTY_IMAGE at an image you have, log in to the registry, or use --runtime native.

Since 0.7 narratty warns when the image runs another narratty version than the command line (an edge image older than your development build, an override with --image): the image may not know keys the spec uses. It asks the image once per image ID. Errors from inside the container name your spec's path, not /spec/….

Each image build gets its own ID (/opt/narratty/image-id), and narratty passes the local image ID to the container as NARRATTY_IMAGE_ID. The scene cache keys recordings to both, so footage recorded with one image, its fonts and its browser is not reused with a rebuilt one.

docs.title: What the container can see
docs.text:
Host Container Access the spec file /spec/<name> read-only the prepared workspace (see below) /work read-write, or read-only with ro the output file's directory /out read-write the audio and scene caches /cache read-write, shared with native runs your downloaded voices /data read-only

Voices are downloaded on the host before the container starts. The container runs with no network, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges, a read-only root filesystem and your own user id, so files it writes belong to you. With rootless Docker, where the container's root is your user, it runs as root for the same reason (since 0.5).

docs.title: Workspace modes
docs.text:
workspace.mode decides what directory the demo runs in. --workspace-mode overrides it for one run.

Mode Runs in Use it when snapshot (default) a throwaway copy: for git repositories a local clone of HEAD plus your uncommitted and untracked files (not ignored ones) the demo builds or writes files; your checkout stays untouched rw the real directory build results should stay in the repository; refused on a tree with uncommitted changes unless --allow-dirty, and afterwards narratty lists the files the demo changed ro the real directory, read-only the demo only reads; enforced in the container only

--keep-workspace keeps the snapshot (under the cache directory) for inspection. A build stopped with Ctrl+C or kill (SIGTERM) removes its container and snapshot (since 0.7). workspace.include_uncommitted: false snapshots exactly HEAD.

Files the demo produces can be copied out with workspace.artifacts, a list of globs relative to the workspace. They land next to the video in <name>.artifacts/.

workspace.caches maps a name to a directory inside the container (e.g. bazel: ~/.cache/bazel). Each is a directory under the cache directory on the host that persists across runs, so builds in the demo stay fast. In native mode your real cache directories are used.

docs.title: Sandbox permissions
docs.text:
A spec declares what else the demo needs:

sandbox:
  network: allowlist               # none (default) | allowlist | full
  allow_hosts:
    - license.example.com:27000
    - cache.example.com:443
  env_passthrough: [LM_LICENSE_FILE]   # copied from your shell, never stored in the spec
  env: {TZ: UTC}
  extra_mounts:
    - {host: ~/.netrc, container: ~/.netrc, mode: ro}
  ssh_agent: false
  docker: false
  • network: allowlist puts the container on an internal network with no route out. For each allowed host a small forwarder (in the same image) joins that network under the host's name and passes its ports through to the real host, which narratty resolves on your machine. TCP is forwarded as is, so licence servers, TLS (with SNI and certificates intact) and other protocols work without proxy settings. Nothing else is reachable.
  • network: full uses the container runtime's normal network.
  • --network none|allowlist|full and --allow-host HOST:PORT (repeatable) override the spec for one run.

docs.title: Docker in the demo
docs.text:
docker: true mounts your Docker or Podman engine's socket into the container. The demo's docker and docker compose commands then start containers on your machine, next to the narratty container.

This is full access to your machine

Whoever can use the engine can start a privileged container that mounts /. Use it only for specs you trust. The approval prompt says so, and allow_docker = false in the policy blocks it for every spec.

  • The socket is DOCKER_HOST (a unix:// path) or /var/run/docker.sock for Docker, and CONTAINER_HOST or the socket podman info reports for Podman (systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket).
  • The workspace is mounted at its path on the host instead of /work, so bind mounts the demo passes to the engine (-v .:/app, Compose volumes:) point at the same files.
  • Containers the demo starts use the engine's networks, not the sandbox's. A port they publish is on your machine, not on localhost in the narratty container; use docker compose exec to work inside them.
  • They keep running after the render. Stop them in a hidden last scene (docker compose down).

docs.title: You stay in control
docs.text:
The first run of a spec that asks for more than the defaults lists what it wants and asks for approval. The answer is remembered for that spec file and that exact sandbox block, so a changed spec asks again. Pass --yes (or set NARRATTY_YES=1) in CI.

A policy in ~/.config/narratty/config.toml caps what any spec may get:

[sandbox]
max_network = "allowlist"          # none | allowlist | full
allow_env = ["LM_LICENSE_FILE"]    # env_passthrough names a spec may use
allow_mounts = true
allow_ssh_agent = false
allow_docker = false

A spec that needs more than the policy allows fails with a message naming what is over the limit.

In native mode none of this can be enforced: the demo runs with your own network and environment, and narratty says so. sandbox.env is still applied. env_passthrough is not needed there either, since the demo sees your whole environment, so native runs ask for no approval.

Hidden commands run natively on your machine too, with your own HOME, and narratty says so once. Since 0.7 a hidden command that points at your home directory (git config --global, ~/…, $HOME) stops a native check or build before anything runs, unless you pass --yes; in the container it changes only the container's throwaway home.

docs.title: Docs for reading and listening
docs.text:
A narratty doc serves two audiences from one file: someone reading it in a browser and someone watching the video. The goal is one source of truth: plain Markdown that reads well, with as few <!-- narratty: … --> comments as possible. Every comment is a "parallel world" that readers don't see and that can drift from the text around it.

This page collects the rules that keep the two in step. They come from two rounds of a usability study in which authors wrote tutorials, architecture overviews and runbooks with narratty and retrofitted existing guides to it.

docs.title: The scene model in one paragraph
docs.text: The doc is read top to bottom. The paragraph directly before a block is its lead-in and is spoken while that block runs; by default narration and typing start together. A paragraph after a block is spoken in the next scene, while the output is still on screen. A run comment before a block changes the order per block, see Choosing who goes first. See also How a doc becomes scenes.

docs.title: Write for the ear first, then check the page
docs.text:
1. Keep the lead-in short and end it with a colon. One or two sentences that say what the command does: "Check that it works:". The colon also tells narratty the paragraph belongs to the next block or slide, and listeners that something follows.
  2. Explain output after the block. A paragraph after a block is spoken while the output is on screen. That is the natural "run, then explain".
  3. Avoid spatial and UI words. "Above", "below", "the command below" and "click here" make no sense when spoken; narratty validate flags them. Reword ("next", "this command", "the output shows") rather than adding a skip + say pair.
  4. Let callouts speak for themselves. Warning, caution, danger and important admonitions start with their type and title ("Warning: Cache keys. …"). Note and tip are read like text. Change it per type with the entry key admonitions.
  5. Footnotes and task lists are fine. Markers and checkboxes are not spoken; footnotes are skipped, or spoken after their sentence with footnotes: inline.
  6. Spell out what TTS gets wrong in the lexicon, not in the text. Run narratty lexicon check and add terms such as JWT or config.yaml to tts.lexicon in the spec comment. The text stays correct for readers.

docs.title: Keep the reader's commands as readers type them
docs.text:
1. Label every shell fence console, with $ prompts and the real output. Volatile parts become ..., also within a line (Python 3...).
  2. Never rewrite a command for the video. Use a run comment instead:
  3. until: "listening on" for tail -f and servers: wait for the text, then Ctrl+C;
  4. lines: 10 to shorten long output on screen (check still compares the full output);
  5. instead: "pip install -e ." when the reader's command can't run in the demo (offline install, a clone of their fork).
  6. Make expected failures fail for real and mark them expect-failure. check verifies both the exit code and the output.
  7. Redirect the output of background jobs (app > app.log 2>&1 &). Output that arrives after the prompt can make a build time out; validate warns about a bare &.
  8. Write placeholders as environment variables ($TOKEN, not <token>). Put values in sandbox.env or sandbox.env_passthrough, never in a hidden block.
  9. Use no-run for host-only commands (sudo, editors, open). The command stays on screen without being run; say in the text that it is shown, or add an overlay.

docs.title: Keep the parallel world small
docs.text:
1. Prefer a Markdown construct over a comment. A table with a table comment, a diagram with focus comments and a heading per step read well on the page. A say that replaces a paragraph does not.
  2. Show snippets that aren't project files with narratty="show". A JSON response or a config excerpt becomes a highlighted code slide; don't invent a title for it.
  3. Let slides stay for their conclusion with hold: next-block or hold: next-heading on the slide or table comment.
  4. Clear the screen with clear_on: 2 in the spec comment instead of hidden clear commands.
  5. Keep setup out of the doc. Toolchains go into environment, variables and git identity into sandbox.env. If a hidden block is unavoidable, keep it to one at the top of the first section, and never let it touch $HOME or use --global: under --runtime native it runs on your machine.
  6. Pick sections, don't skip paragraphs. sections: {exclude: [troubleshooting]} keeps the intro; <!-- narratty: skip-rest --> leaves out the rest of a section.
  7. Remove old workarounds when you upgrade. A say Warning! or a footnote skip + say from before 0.7 now doubles up with the new defaults.

docs.title: Check before you build
docs.text:
1. Run narratty validate, then narratty check, after every edit. Treat each warning as a to-do item. check runs the commands as the video would and reports "N commands ran, M shown only"; nothing ran means nothing is wired up.
  2. Run narratty plan --sources to see what each Markdown element became and why something was left out. Run check first: plan then uses the measured command durations.
  3. Look at the video at section changes and after slides. Extract frames with ffmpeg -ss <t> -i out.mp4 -frames:v 1 f.png, and read the .srt.

docs.title: What each element becomes
docs.text: Element On the page In the video Recommendation Heading Structure Chapter overlay (heading_overlays); the H1 card stays during the intro One heading per step; it also scopes sections Paragraph Text Lead-in of the next block, or the scene after a block Short before a block, explanations after it console block Command and output Typed, run, output compared by check The default for shell examples bash block Script Each command runs; output not compared Scripts readers copy as a whole Code with title File listing Written hidden, shown with cat and a file overlay Config files the demo needs Code with narratty="show" Listing Highlighted code slide Responses, excerpts, examples Code without either Listing Left out (validate warns) Add show or a title Table Table Left out; slide with a table or slide comment Decisions and comparisons: table {say: "If {A}, {B}."} mermaid Diagram Slide; focus comments walk flowchart nodes and sequence participants One short paragraph per node Image on its own line Image Slide titled with the alt text Write a meaningful alt text Admonition Callout Warnings say their type and title Nothing extra needed Collapsed block, <details> Hidden until opened Left out Reader-only background, FAQ Content tabs Tabs First tab, or the one the entry names Keep tabs equivalent Footnote, task list Rendered Markers not spoken Fine Inline code, links Formatted Plain text, lexicon applies Avoid bare URLs

docs.title: Choosing who goes first: voice or command
docs.text:
You want Write before the block What happens Talk while it runs nothing Default (say: during) Explain, then run <!-- narratty: run {say: before} --> Typing starts once the lead-in is spoken Run, then explain in the same scene <!-- narratty: run {say: after} --> The text after the block is spoken once the commands are done Let the output sink in <!-- narratty: pause 2s --> after the block A silent pause

The same keys fit in the block's attributes (narratty="say=before lines=10"), and the entry key say: before makes "explain, then run" the default for a whole tutorial. With say: after, keep the lead-in very short: it is spoken over an idle prompt.

docs.title: Retrofitting an existing guide
docs.text:
1. Run narratty validate on the guide as it is. Typical result: "no command runs" and one warning per unlabelled fence with $ lines.
  2. Label shell fences console; replace volatile output with ....
  3. Split blocks so that commands with different needs (run, no-run, instead) are in separate blocks, and turn commands that only appear inline in a step ("run make lint") into blocks. Both help readers too.
  4. Mark host-only steps no-run; use instead for steps that need another command in the demo, until for commands that don't end.
  5. Make sure every section's first block has a lead-in, or it plays silent.
  6. Set clear_on: 2, pick the sections with sections: {exclude: [...]}, and add environment.packages when check reports a missing tool (exit 127).
  7. Add a table comment to tables the video needs and focus comments to diagrams.
  8. Run check, then build, and look at the frames at each section change.

Expect to change about a sixth of the reader-visible text, and most of those changes improve the written guide as well.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: The repository ships an agent skill that applies these rules when writing or retrofitting a doc: skills/narratty-docs/SKILL.md. Copy it into your agent's skill directory (for Claude Code, .claude/skills/narratty-docs/).

docs.title: Project environments
docs.text:
By default the demo shell runs in the narratty image. When the demo needs your project's own toolchain, run the shell in the project's image or Compose service instead. Only the shell moves: VHS, Chromium, the voices and ffmpeg stay in narratty, and the project's image needs no change.

environment:
  image: ghcr.io/acme/toolchain:2.3
  workdir: /work        # where the workspace is mounted and the shell starts
  user: host            # host (default) | image | UID[:GID]

The image needs Linux (amd64 or arm64) and the terminal.shell. Without environment, nothing changes. --runtime native only decides where narratty's own tools run: the demo shell still starts in the environment, and the log says so. Pass --no-env to run the demo shell on this machine instead. Set exactly one source:

Source Use it for image A ready image, nothing else to configure compose Everything else: a Dockerfile, mounts, networks, users, several services container A container that is already running

A Dockerfile, a docker run command or a dev container all become a few lines of Compose; see From Dockerfile, docker run or dev container.

docs.title: Run in a Compose service
docs.text:
environment:
  compose:
    file: compose.yaml    # relative to the spec
    service: dev

narratty starts the Compose project from the workspace (a snapshot by default), so the service's relative mounts such as .:/src point at it. It waits until the services are up (up --wait), runs the demo shell in dev, and removes the project with its volumes afterwards. The shell starts in the service's working_dir unless workdir is set. Networks, mounts and privileges come from the Compose file, including network_mode: host; the sandbox rules do not apply to them.

file also takes a list ([compose.yaml, compose.dev.yaml]), merged in order like repeated docker compose -f.

docs.title: From Dockerfile, docker run or dev container
docs.text:
Compose describes how to build and start a container, so narratty needs nothing else.

A Dockerfile:

# compose.yaml
services:
  dev:
    build: {context: ., dockerfile: docker/dev.Dockerfile, target: dev, args: {PY: "3.12"}}
    command: sleep infinity
    volumes: [".:/src"]
    working_dir: /src

A docker run --network host -v .:/src -w /src -u 1000 -e TZ=UTC acme/dev sleep infinity:

services:
  dev:
    image: acme/dev
    command: sleep infinity
    network_mode: host
    volumes: [".:/src"]
    working_dir: /src
    user: "1000"
    environment: {TZ: UTC}

A dev container with dockerComposeFile already has one: point environment.compose at it. For one with only image or build, write the Compose file as above with its workspaceFolder as working_dir. Editor extensions, features and lifecycle commands (postCreateCommand, ...) are not used; put what the demo needs into the Dockerfile, or into packages and setup (see Extra tools).

docs.title: Example: record a build in the dev container
docs.text:
examples/devcontainer is a small project whose dev container is a Compose service. The spec points at that Compose file; the video runs the real build inside the container:

devcontainer.jsoncompose.yamldemo.narratty.yaml 
// The project's dev container, as VS Code and the Dev Container CLI use it.
{
  "name": "greeter",
  "dockerComposeFile": "compose.yaml",
  "service": "dev",
  "workspaceFolder": "/workspace",
}

services:
  dev:
    build:
      context: ..
      dockerfile: .devcontainer/Dockerfile
    command: sleep infinity
    volumes:
      - ..:/workspace
    working_dir: /workspace
    environment:
      APP_ENV: demo

meta: {title: Build in the dev container}
terminal: {height: 600}
environment:
  compose:                      # the Compose file the dev container uses
    file: .devcontainer/compose.yaml
    service: dev
scenes:
  - id: intro
    narration: This shell runs in the project's dev container, started from its Compose file.
    actions:
      - run: python --version && echo "APP_ENV=$APP_ENV"
  - id: tree
    narration: The project is mounted where the dev container expects it.
    actions:
      - run: pwd && eza --tree --level 2
  - id: build
    narration: Now the real build runs. The recording waits until it has finished.
    actions:
      - run: python build.py
      - wait: {prompt: true, timeout_ms: 600000}
  - id: result
    narration: The build wrote into a copy of the project, so your checkout stays clean.
    actions:
      - run: cat dist/report.txt
  1. Check what the demo will see: narratty env shell demo.narratty.yaml opens the shell the recording gets. Try the commands there.
  2. Iterate quickly: narratty env up demo.narratty.yaml keeps the container running, so narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --draft skips the start-up each time.
  3. Record: narratty build demo.narratty.yaml, then narratty env down demo.narratty.yaml.

wait: {prompt: true} waits until the build has finished, however long it takes (up to timeout_ms). With the default snapshot workspace the build writes into a copy, so the checkout stays clean. eza comes from the demo toolkit, not from the dev container.

docs.title: Run in a running container
docs.text:
environment:
  container: dev        # name or id
  user: image
workspace:
  mode: rw              # required: the demo works in the container's own files

narratty neither starts nor stops the container and adds no mounts; the demo shell starts in its working directory. Use this for a dev container you already have open.

docs.title: Extra tools for the demo
docs.text:
When the image lacks tools the demo shows, packages adds them with the image's package manager and setup runs further commands:

environment:
  image: ghcr.io/acme/toolchain:2.3   # or compose
  packages: [bat, jq, tree]
  package_manager: auto               # auto | apt | apk | dnf | microdnf | yum | zypper
  setup:
    - curl -fsSL https://example.com/tool.tar.gz | tar -xz -C /usr/local/bin

narratty builds a small image on top: root and network access only while building, then the image's own user again. It is tagged narratty-env:<hash> of the base image, the packages and the commands, so a second run builds nothing. auto detects the package manager once per image; an image without one (distroless, scratch) needs setup or its own Dockerfile. narratty env build SPEC builds ahead of time (for image), --rebuild-env forces a rebuild.

Because the build runs as root with network access, the first run asks for approval, like sandbox permissions. packages and setup work with image and compose, not with a running container.

docs.title: Demo toolkit
docs.text: The toolkit (yazi, bat, eza and their settings) is mounted read-only at /.narratty/toolkit and put first on PATH; nothing is installed into the image. toolkit: fallback puts it last, so the image's own tools win; toolkit: off leaves it out. Without the toolkit image (offline, no access to GHCR) the demo runs without it.

docs.title: Editor layout and diff
docs.text:
Both are plain shell commands, so they need no narratty in the container.

  • terminal.layout: editor with image or compose: tmux and yazi run next to narratty (they are in the narratty image and the native install's PATH); only the terminal pane opens the shell in the environment. reveal and diff see the same workspace on both sides.
  • With container, narratty shares no workspace with the container, so the whole layout runs in it. It needs tmux, yazi and ya there. To use the toolkit, start the container from a Compose file instead.
  • diff outside the editor layout runs in the environment's shell and needs git there.

A missing tool fails the build with a message that names it and where it is missing.

docs.title: Keep it running
docs.text:
narratty env up demo.narratty.yaml     # start and keep the environment
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml      # uses it: no start-up, warm state
narratty env shell demo.narratty.yaml  # look around in the same container
narratty env down demo.narratty.yaml   # remove container, volumes and snapshot

While it runs, build, render and env shell reuse it instead of starting a new one. The demo then sees what earlier runs left behind, so reset state in a hidden scene when a video must start clean.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text:
1. narratty pulls or builds the image, prepares the workspace and starts the image with the workspace mounted at workdir (or starts the Compose service, or attaches to the container).
  2. In a sandboxed run, the static narratty-agent from the narratty image is mounted read-only into that container. It serves the demo shell over a socket in a small volume shared with the narratty container, which keeps no network and no access to Docker. For a running container the agent is copied in, serves one shell on an abstract socket and is removed afterwards. In a native run, docker exec opens the shell.
  3. The recording types into that shell. The end card is drawn by narratty after the demo shell has exited.
  4. The container is removed afterwards. --keep-env keeps it and prints how to enter it. A running container is left as it was.

docs.title: Rules and permissions
docs.text:
The sandbox applies to the environment's container, in native runs too: network, allow_hosts, env, env_passthrough, extra_mounts, ssh_agent and workspace.caches. All capabilities are dropped and no-new-privileges is set.

user Runs as ~ in mounts and caches host your user id; files the demo writes belong to you /home/narratty (a tmpfs, also $HOME) image the image's USER the image's $HOME UID[:GID] or a name that user the image's $HOME

env sets variables in the environment's container (not for container). read_only: true also mounts the image's root filesystem read-only (off by default, since project images often write outside the workspace).

compose and container run with what the Compose file or the container already has, so the first run asks for approval for them too.

A policy in ~/.config/narratty/config.toml limits which kinds of environments a spec may use:

[sandbox]
allow_environment = ["image"]   # also "compose", "container"; [] forbids all
allow_packages = false                   # no packages or setup commands

docs.title: Builds with a warm cache
docs.text:
Keep the checkout clean and the build fast: the default snapshot workspace gives the build a writable copy, and workspace.caches keeps caches across runs in directories under narratty's cache directory.

workspace:
  mode: snapshot                      # default; writes never reach your checkout
  caches: {bazel: ~/.cache/bazel}     # persists between runs
environment:
  image: ghcr.io/acme/toolchain:2.3

For a long build, wait: {prompt: true, timeout_ms: 900000} waits until the command has finished and the prompt is back.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml                          # environment from the spec
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --env-image acme/dev:2   # another image for this run
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --no-env                 # demo in the narratty image
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --keep-env               # keep the container afterwards
narratty build demo.narratty.yaml --rebuild-env            # rebuild Dockerfile and packages
narratty env build demo.narratty.yaml                      # build the image only
narratty env shell demo.narratty.yaml                      # interactive shell, same setup
narratty env up demo.narratty.yaml                         # start and keep it
narratty env down demo.narratty.yaml                       # remove it

narratty env shell starts the environment like a build would, with the same bridge, and opens an interactive terminal.shell in it, to check what the demo will see.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Initialisation from the image's ENTRYPOINT (for example conda activate) does not run; the container starts terminal.shell directly. Put that setup into a hidden scene.
  • An image for another architecture runs under emulation, which is slow.
  • Windows containers are not supported.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
narratty needs Python 3.12 or newer.

uv tool install narratty
# or
pipx install narratty

docs.title: Runtimes
docs.text:
narratty runs the recording pipeline either natively (tools on your PATH) or sandboxed in a container. By default (--runtime auto) it uses Docker when it is installed, then Podman, and falls back to native mode with a warning.

Runtime You need docker / podman Docker or Podman native vhs, ttyd, ffmpeg (with ffprobe), git; Piper is installed with narratty

See Sandboxed runs for what the container sees and which image is used.

Run narratty doctor to see what your runtime needs and what is missing. Pick a runtime with --runtime or the NARRATTY_RUNTIME environment variable.

macOS

macOS support is best effort. Native mode works when the tools above are installed with Homebrew; sandboxed mode works through Docker Desktop or Podman.

docs.title: Markdown input
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.5.

A Markdown doc can be the source of a video, so one file is both read and watched. Paragraphs become the narration, code blocks become what the video types and runs. Plain docs need no extra markup. Comments and code block attributes, both invisible on the rendered page, change what the video does where the defaults don't fit.

This is the recommended way to use narratty. The doc stays the source: readers read it, others watch or listen to the video. Every command runs while the video is recorded, and narratty check also compares what the commands print with the doc (see Checking docs in CI). A doc can be built on its own; a YAML spec that points at it adds scenes before and after it, or combines several docs.

The video is made from this page; its spec is examples/markdown/markdown.narratty.yaml.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Write the doc as usual. This one says hello in the terminal.

hello.md
# Hello

Say hello to the terminal.

```console
$ echo "Hello from Markdown"
```

A spec points at the doc with a markdown entry in its scenes. The entry turns into ordinary scenes, so hand-written scenes can stand before and after it.

hello.narratty.yaml
scenes:
  - markdown: hello.md

narratty compile prints the scenes the doc turns into. The paragraph is the narration, and the console line is a command that runs.

$ narratty compile hello.narratty.yaml
scenes:
  # from hello.md:5
  - id: hello-1
    narration: Say hello to the terminal.
    actions:
      - run: echo "Hello from Markdown"
      - wait: {prompt: true}

narratty plan --sources lists where each scene comes from, and what was left out and why.

$ narratty plan --sources hello.narratty.yaml

Build the video like any other spec:

$ narratty build hello.narratty.yaml

docs.title: Building a doc on its own
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

Every command that takes a spec also takes a Markdown doc:

narratty build hello.md      # writes hello.mp4
narratty check hello.md      # runs the commands and compares their output

The doc then implies its spec: a single markdown entry for the whole doc. Its commands run in a copy of the doc's git repository, from the root, or in the doc's folder outside a repository. A spec comment sets other keys, those of the spec and those of the markdown entry:

<!-- narratty: spec
tts: {voice: am_michael}
heading_overlays: 2
sandbox: {network: full}
-->

The comment is YAML, invisible on the page like the other comments, and problems in it are reported at their line in the doc. It cannot hold scenes, and a YAML spec that points at the doc ignores it.

Write a YAML spec when the video needs more than the doc: scenes before or after it, several docs, or several videos from one doc. narratty init --markdown hello.md writes one to start from.

docs.title: How a doc becomes scenes
docs.text:
The doc is read in order. Paragraphs collect until a code block runs; then they are the narration of the scene that runs it.

Markdown In the video Paragraphs before a code block, same section The narration of the scene that runs the block Paragraphs after the last block of a section A scene without actions; the output stays on screen A block without a paragraph before it A silent scene console block $ lines run, > lines right after them continue them; other lines are output, not typed, and compared by narratty check bash / sh block Each complete command runs (heredocs, if, for stay together); # … comments are not typed Other language with a title Written to that file (hidden), then shown with cat and a file overlay Any language with narratty="show" Shown as a highlighted code slide while the text around it is spoken; nothing is written or run (since 0.7), see Code shown, not run Other language without a title Left out Inline code, links, emphasis Read as plain text, so the lexicon applies to inline code too List items Read as sentences; a code block in an item runs like any other Task list items - [ ], - [x] Read without the box (since 0.7) Footnotes [^1] The marker is not read, the footnote itself not spoken (since 0.7), see Footnotes Quotes and GitHub alerts (> [!NOTE]) Read like paragraphs, without the [!NOTE] marker; [!WARNING], [!CAUTION] and [!IMPORTANT] start with their type (since 0.7) Admonitions !!! and open collapsible blocks ???+ Read without their title; warning, caution, danger and important start with their type and title (since 0.7); code blocks inside run as usual Collapsed blocks ??? and <details> Left out, with everything inside Content tabs === "…" One tab per tab set, see below An image on a line of its own Shown as a slide, titled with its alt text, while the text around it is spoken, see Images mermaid block Drawn as a slide (since 0.6), see Slides Tables Left out; with a table comment spoken row by row, with a slide comment shown (since 0.6), see Tables Images within text (badges), raw HTML Left out

Text after a slide (an image, diagram, code slide or table shown) or after a block with say: after belongs to it, up to the next block. The paragraph right before the next block introduces that block instead (since 0.7): it narrates the next command or slide when it ends with a colon, such as "Pipe it to head:", or when other paragraphs come before it. A single paragraph without a colon stays with the slide.

Every command waits until the prompt is back, so the next one starts after it has finished. A command that fails stops the build, as in a YAML spec; mark the block expect-failure when that is the point (see Code block attributes).

Scene ids are <file stem>-<heading>-<n>, for example install-uv-2; a heading whose slug is the file stem is left out (install-1, not install-install-1). A block with an id uses <file stem>-<id>, which survives edits around it. id_prefix replaces the file stem.

docs.title: Callouts and tabs
docs.text:
Admonitions are spoken without their title, so a tip reads as part of the text.

Short paragraphs

Keep paragraphs short. Each one is a sentence or two of narration.

Warnings are different: a listener cannot see the box. Since 0.7, warning, caution, danger and important admonitions and alerts start with their type and, if given, their title.

Slow first build

The first build downloads the voice.

The video says "Warning: Slow first build. The first build downloads the voice." admonitions in the entry changes the start per type, with a template of {type}, {title} (the title, else the type) and {body}; admonitions: false reads every type without a start.

- markdown: docs/install.md
  admonitions:
    tip: "Tip: {body}"          # tips say so too
    warning: "Careful: {body}"  # instead of "Warning: <title>. <body>"
    important: "{body}"         # no start

Collapsed blocks are for readers only. The video leaves them out, with everything inside, including code blocks.

Only on the page

This text and the command below are not part of the video.

$ echo "only for readers"

This is how both look in the doc.

callouts.md
!!! tip "Short paragraphs"
    Keep paragraphs short. Each one is a sentence or two of narration.

??? note "Only on the page"
    This text and the command below are not part of the video.

Content tabs show one tab in the video: the first, or the first label the entry lists in tabs. This video picks the bash tab.

zshbash 
$ echo "$ZSH_VERSION"

$ echo "$BASH_VERSION"

Collapsible blocks that start open are spoken like admonitions. HTML details blocks are left out like collapsed ones.

docs.title: Footnotes
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.7.

Footnote markers are not read, and the footnotes themselves are not spoken: they are asides for readers.1 footnotes: inline in the entry speaks each footnote right after the sentence that refers to it.

The cache is shared between builds.[^1]

[^1]: Each build only adds the scenes that changed.

With footnotes: inline the video says "The cache is shared between builds. Each build only adds the scenes that changed."

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
An image on a line of its own is shown as a slide while the text around it is spoken. Its alt text is the slide's title (since 0.7); image_titles: false in the entry leaves titles out, and a slide comment's title replaces it.

The image stays until the next command or heading, so it never covers what is typed. It is embedded in the spec, which keeps it working in the sandbox without network.

Images within a sentence (such as badges), remote images and formats other than PNG, JPEG, GIF, SVG and WebP are left out. images: false in the entry leaves out all images, and a skip comment a single one. A slide comment gives it a title, see Slides.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

A table is left out of the video unless a comment stands before it. With a table comment it is shown as a slide, and its rows are spoken one by one, each highlighted while it is spoken.

Step Command Shows Check narratty validate problems, at the Markdown file and line Preview narratty plan --sources where each scene comes from Build narratty build the finished video

This is the comment that stands before the table.

<!-- narratty: table {say: "{Step}: {Command} shows {Shows}.", title: From doc to video} -->
| Step | Command | Shows |

For a voiceover that does not read the cells, give say one phrase per row. The snippet configures the spoken steps; the live table after it is what those steps highlight:

<!-- narratty: table {title: Request path, say: ["The client sends a request.", "The API checks the request.", "The database stores the result."]} -->
| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| Client | Sends a request to the API |
| API | Checks the request |
| Database | Stores the result |
Step What happens Client Sends a request to the API API Checks the request Database Stores the result
  • Without say, each cell is read with its header, such as "Step: Check.", and empty cells are left out.
  • say fills in the cells of the columns named in braces; names match the header regardless of case.
  • say: ["First custom narration.", "Second custom narration."] supplies one custom phrase per row; the list must have exactly as many phrases as the table has rows (since 0.7).
  • pause: 500ms highlights each row that long before it is spoken.
  • title, theme and rows set the look of the slide, as in the slide comment; hold keeps it up after its rows, see How long a slide stays.
  • Cells are read like paragraphs, so the lexicon applies to inline code in them.
  • A paragraph right before the comment that ends with a colon, such as "The steps are:", introduces the table: it is spoken with the first row, while the slide is shown (since 0.7). Other paragraphs are spoken before the slide appears.

A slide comment shows a table without reading it, while the text after it is spoken. rows: 8 splits a long table into pages of 8 rows; each pause comment in the text after it brings up the next page, and pages left when the text ends follow for a few seconds each.

<!-- narratty: slide {title: All hazards, rows: 8} -->
| Hazard | Severity | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| … |

The first eight hazards concern the machine itself.

<!-- narratty: pause -->

The next ones concern the workplace around it.

docs.title: Pauses
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

Paragraphs that follow each other are spoken in one go, up to the next code block. A pause comment ends the scene where it stands, and with a duration silence follows.

This paragraph comes after a second of silence.

Paragraphs that follow each other are spoken in one go.

<!-- narratty: pause 1s -->

This paragraph comes after a second of silence.

Without a duration, pause only ends the scene; the next one follows after timing.narration_buffer_ms. A horizontal rule (---) does not end a scene. While a table with pages is shown, a pause brings up its next page.

docs.title: Slides
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

Tables, mermaid blocks and images become slides: shown full screen while the text around them is spoken, dark unless the spec sets slides: {theme: light}. GitHub draws mermaid blocks too, and so does mkdocs with the mermaid custom fence of pymdownx.superfences.

flowchart LR
  doc[Markdown doc] --> entry[markdown entry] --> scenes --> video

A slide comment before a table, diagram or image sets its title and look; focus emphasizes a Mermaid node or subgraph while the scene is narrated.

<!-- narratty: slide {title: From doc to video, theme: light} -->
Key Does title Text above the content theme dark or light for this slide rows Table rows per page, see Tables focus Mermaid node or subgraph ID to emphasize (since 0.7) hold Keeps the slide up for the text after it: next-block or next-heading (since 0.7), see How long a slide stays html Shows an HTML file instead, from the next paragraph on

For a voiceover walkthrough in Markdown, write the Mermaid diagram once, then use a focus comment for each later step. The comment closes the previous narration scene without adding silence. Here is the source snippet:

<!-- narratty: slide {title: Request flow, focus: api} -->
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  api[API] --> db[Database]
```
The API receives the request.

<!-- narratty: focus db -->
The database stores it.

And here is the same Markdown as live content, which renders the diagram:

flowchart LR
  api[API] --> db[Database]
The API receives the request.

The database stores it.

The focus comment (since 0.7) closes the previous narration scene and reuses the last Mermaid diagram with a new focus target. It takes one node or subgraph ID from the diagram source, such as db or api-gateway. The diagram must still be on screen: a heading, table, image, browser view or command block in between ends it. With narration: none and no say text before it, or with images: false, the comment is left out like the diagram. In YAML, repeat the slide action in one scene per focus ID instead. A node stays emphasized for its scene's narration unless duration_ms caps the slide. In a sequence diagram, focus takes a participant's ID, such as C for participant C as Client, and emphasizes both of its boxes (since 0.7).

Mermaid labels can use Unicode emoji; the narratty image includes an emoji font. Its bundled Font Awesome 6 Solid icons use the fa: prefix, for example fa:server in Mermaid's icon syntax. Native renders can set NARRATTY_FONTAWESOME_JSON to an Iconify-compatible Font Awesome icons.json file. The bundled icons are Font Awesome Free by Fonticons, Inc., licensed under CC BY 4.0.

Diagrams are drawn when the video is rendered, with the mermaid.min.js that comes with the narratty image, so they need no network. Native renders read it from NARRATTY_MERMAID_JS or from the data directory; narratty doctor shows where. images: false leaves out diagrams too.

docs.title: How long a slide stays
docs.text:
A slide is shown while the text around it is spoken, up to the next block, heading or pause comment; a scene after that shows the terminal again. hold keeps the slide up for more of the text after it (since 0.7):

hold The slide stays for the text after it, up to unset the end of its scene next-block the next command or file block, slide, browser view or heading; pause comments in between keep it next-heading the next heading, slide or browser view; it gives way to commands while they run and comes back for the text after them 
<!-- narratty: slide {title: Request path, hold: next-block} -->

A table comment takes hold too: the table stays, without a highlighted row, for the text after its rows. In YAML, repeat the slide action in each scene instead.

A slide made in HTML is named with html, relative to the doc:

<!-- narratty: slide {html: slides/architecture.html} -->
The architecture has three parts.

Like an image, the page is embedded in the spec, so it must be self-contained: styles inline, images inline as SVG or data: URLs.

docs.title: Code shown, not run
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.7.

A block marked narratty="show" is shown as a syntax-highlighted slide while the text around it is spoken, like an image. Nothing is written or run, so it suits an API response or a config excerpt that is not a file in the project:

The health endpoint answers with the version:

{"status": "ok", "version": "0.7.0"}

This is its source:

```json {narratty="show"}
{"status": "ok", "version": "0.7.0"}
```

show works with any language, also console (then nothing runs). A title becomes the slide title, and a slide comment before the block sets its title and theme.

docs.title: Doc comments
docs.text:
HTML comments are invisible on the docs site and on GitHub. Those starting with narratty: hold what only the video needs:

<!-- narratty: skip -->
This paragraph is only for readers.

<!-- narratty: say
Narration only the video has. It may span lines.
-->

<!-- narratty: overlay {text: compose.yaml, style: file} -->

<!-- narratty: hidden
git init demo && cd demo
-->

<!-- narratty: browser {scroll: auto, duration_ms: 6s} -->
The [Compose file reference](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) lists every key.

<!-- narratty: pause 800ms -->

<!-- narratty: table {say: "{Hazard}: {Mitigation}"} -->
| Hazard | Mitigation |

<!-- narratty: slide {title: Architecture} -->
![The parts](architecture.svg)
Comment Does skip Leaves the next paragraph or block out of the video; before a heading, its overlay skip-rest Leaves the rest of the section out, up to the next heading of the same or a higher level (since 0.7) say Adds narration where it stands; skip plus say replaces a paragraph overlay Shows an overlay in the next scene; takes the same value as the action, and text with a colon such as not run: in this video stays text (since 0.7) hidden Runs setup commands in the recorded shell without showing them browser Opens a link of the next paragraph in a browser view, see Opening links pause Ends the scene; with a duration, silence follows (since 0.6), see Pauses table Speaks the next table row by row on a slide (since 0.6), see Tables slide Sets the title and look of the next table, diagram or image, or shows an HTML file (since 0.6), see Slides focus Reuses the last Mermaid diagram, emphasizing the given node or subgraph for the next narrated step (since 0.7), see Slides clear Clears the screen (since 0.7), see Clearing the screen run How the next shell or console block runs: narration order, a substitute command, output lines, stopping it (since 0.7), see Running commands spec Spec keys for building the doc on its own (since 0.6), see Building a doc on its own

HTML comments cannot contain --; put such text into a YAML scene instead.

docs.title: Opening links
docs.text:
Links are read as plain text. A browser comment opens one of them in a browser view while its paragraph is spoken:

<!-- narratty: browser {scroll: auto, duration_ms: 6s} -->
The [Compose file reference](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) lists every key.
  • Without link it opens the first link of the next paragraph; link: 2 opens the second, link: "Compose file reference" the one with that text. A URL instead of the mapping, <!-- narratty: browser https://example.com -->, opens that page.
  • The other keys are those of the browser action: scroll, duration_ms and load_ms.
  • The paragraph starts a new scene, so the page appears with it. Like an image, the page stays until the next command or heading at the latest.
  • A relative link to another page of the docs (../user-guide/spec.md#overlays) opens the published page: site_url from mkdocs.yml plus the page's path.
  • Web pages need network access: in the container that is sandbox: {network: full} or an allowlist.

docs.title: Code block attributes
docs.text:
An id and per-block options go into one attribute list after the language. mkdocs uses the id as a link anchor and ignores narratty; GitHub ignores both.

```console {#install narratty="no-run"}
$ uv tool install narratty
```

```yaml {#spec title="demo.narratty.yaml"}
scenes: []
```

narratty="…" takes space-separated options:

Option Does no-run Types the command and leaves it on screen without running it; before 0.7 it was cancelled with a visible ^C hidden Runs the block without showing it (setup) expect-failure The block's commands are expected to fail any-output The output the block shows is not compared (since 0.6), see Checking docs in CI show Shows the block as a code slide instead, see Code shown, not run (since 0.7) say=…, instead=…, lines=…, until=…, then=…, timeout=… The keys of the run comment (since 0.7), see Running commands

Write attributes in braces

mkdocs renders console narratty="no-run" (without braces) as plain text. A brace-less title="…" works on its own, but not together with an id.

docs.title: Running commands
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.7.

A run comment right before a shell or console block says how the video runs it. The block stays what readers copy.

<!-- narratty: run {say: before, lines: 10} -->

The same keys fit in the block's attributes as key=value, quoted like in the shell when the value has spaces. Where both are given, the attribute wins.

```console {narratty="instead='pip install -e .' lines=10"}
$ pip install tally
```
Key Does say When the text is spoken: before, during (default) or after the commands, see Explain, then run instead Shows the block's command, runs this one, see Show one command, run another lines Shows only that many lines of each command's output, see Long output until Waits for this regular expression on screen, then stops the last command, see Commands that keep running then The key that stops it: C-c (default) or a key such as q timeout How long until waits (default 30s)

docs.title: Explain, then run
docs.text:
say The video Narration during (default) Speaks while the commands are typed and run The text before the block before Speaks first, then types the commands The text before the block after Runs the commands, then speaks, in the same scene The text after the block, up to the next block's lead-in, heading or pause; the text before it is spoken on its own first

say: before on the markdown entry makes it the default for every block; a run comment with say: during changes it back for one. In YAML, before is a hold: auto before the first action and after is narration_start: after_actions.

$ echo "Hello from Markdown"
Hello from Markdown

The video printed the greeting before this paragraph was spoken.

<!-- narratty: run {say: after} -->

docs.title: Show one command, run another
docs.text:
instead shows the reader's command and runs another one in its place: the reader's pip install tally can stay in the doc while the video installs from the checkout.

<!-- narratty: run {instead: "pip install -e ."} -->
```console
$ pip install tally
```
  • The block's command is typed, then replaced unseen, and the screen shows it with the output of the command that ran. No ^C and no second command appear.
  • The block must have one command, and instead must fit on one line. The block's command may contain placeholders such as <package>, since it does not run.
