  • narratty check runs the instead command and does not compare its output with the output the block shows, which belongs to the reader's command.
  • A no-run block runs nothing in its place: its command is typed and stays on screen, followed by a fresh prompt, so it can look as if it ran without output. To say so in the video, add an overlay comment, such as <!-- narratty: overlay not run: in this video -->, or say it in the text.

docs.title: Long output
docs.text:
lines: 10 shows the first ten lines of each command's output and ends it with ... (N more lines). The block keeps the output readers see, ... included:

<!-- narratty: run {lines: 3} -->
```console
$ seq 100
1
2
...
```
  • narratty check runs the command as it is and compares all of its output with the block.
  • In the video the output goes through awk. The command then writes to a pipe instead of a terminal, so programs that colour their output only in a terminal print it plain, and stderr is merged into stdout. Commands must fit on one line.

docs.title: Commands that keep running
docs.text:
until waits for a pattern in the output, then stops the block's last command, by default with Ctrl+C, and waits for the prompt. Servers and tail -f stay in the doc as readers type them.

<!-- narratty: run {until: "Serving HTTP", timeout: 20s} -->
```console
$ python -m http.server 8000
Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port 8000 (http://0.0.0.0:8000/) ...
...
```
  • The pattern is a regular expression, matched against the whole screen, so pick one the screen does not show before the command prints it.
  • then: q stops a pager with a key instead; keys are those of the key action, C-… is a Ctrl chord.
  • narratty check waits and stops the command the same way. The exit code of a command stopped with Ctrl+C does not count as a failure. Its output ends with what the command prints when stopped, so end the block's output with ....

docs.title: Clearing the screen
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.7.

The screen keeps what earlier commands printed. A clear comment clears it where it stands, so the text after it does not play over old output:

<!-- narratty: clear -->

clear_on: 2 on the markdown entry clears it where each heading of level 2 or higher starts a section. The screen is cleared when the next visible scene starts, together with its heading overlay, also after a hidden block. Headings before the first visible scene, such as the doc's title, clear nothing. Clearing presses Ctrl+L, which runs no command, so exit codes are checked as before; shell: sh has no line editing and cannot clear this way.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
Write placeholders as environment variables, which readers can set and copy:

$ narratty build "$SPEC" --var target="$TARGET"

The video types $SPEC as written, so values, including secrets, never appear on screen. The value comes from sandbox.env, from sandbox.env_passthrough (you set it on the host) or from a hidden comment with an export. A command to run that still contains a placeholder like <url> is an error with the hint to write it as $URL.

Secrets belong in sandbox.env_passthrough: the value stays in your environment and is never written anywhere. A hidden comment's commands are part of the spec, so they travel with it: narratty keeps them out of error messages and out of exits.log (which records <hidden: scene #n> instead), and removes the compiled spec it mounts into the container after the run, but a kept --work-dir still holds them in its tape. Use a hidden export only for values that are not secret.

docs.title: The markdown entry
docs.text:
A YAML spec decides everything at section level and above: which docs, which sections and in what order, the narration rule and the overlays. Several videos from one doc are several YAML files.

narration: all                      # default for every markdown entry
scenes:
  - markdown: docs/environments.md
    sections: [images, compose]     # nested headings included; unset = whole doc
    heading_overlays: 3
  - id: outro
    narration: That's all you need to get started.
  - markdown: docs/building.md
    narration: none                 # only `say` comments are spoken
    heading_overlays: {levels: 3, breadcrumb: true}
    defaults: {typing_speed_ms: 40}
    overrides:
      install:                      # the block {#install}
        narration: Install it with uv.
        fast: true
        before: [{overlay: "pipx works too"}]
Key Default Meaning markdown required The doc, relative to the spec sections whole doc Headings by TOC slug or title; a list path such as [compose, services] picks one of several equal headings; {include: [...], exclude: [...]} also leaves sections out (since 0.7), see Choosing sections narration spec's narration (all) all speaks every paragraph, none only say comments tabs [] Preferred content tab labels; otherwise each tab set's first tab heading_overlays none Show headings down to this level, see Heading overlays file_titles true Show a file block's title as an overlay images true Show images on a line of their own and mermaid blocks, see Images id_prefix file stem Start of the generated scene ids clear_on none Clear the screen where a heading of this level or higher starts a section (since 0.7), see Clearing the screen say during When the text before a block is spoken: before its commands are typed, or during them (since 0.7), see Explain, then run check_output true Let narratty check compare the output console blocks show, see Checking docs in CI (since 0.6) footnotes skip inline speaks each footnote after the sentence that refers to it, see Footnotes (since 0.7) admonitions {} Per type, how admonitions and alerts start, or false, see Callouts and tabs (since 0.7) image_titles true Use an image's alt text as its slide title, see Images (since 0.7) lint true Let narratty validate warn about the doc, see Checking the result (since 0.7) defaults {} Scene keys for every scene: typing_speed_ms, pause_ms, fast, timelapse, narration_start, expect_exit overrides {} Per block id: the same scene keys plus narration and before / after action lists

A missing section or an override for an id that is not in the doc is an error with a "did you mean".

docs.title: Choosing sections
docs.text:
A list of sections picks them, in that order, with their nested headings. To leave out a section but keep the rest, intro included, exclude it (since 0.7):

- markdown: CONTRIBUTING.md
  sections: {exclude: [faq, troubleshooting]}
- markdown: docs/guide.md
  sections: {include: [install, usage], exclude: [windows]}  # usage without its windows part

Inside the doc, a <!-- narratty: skip-rest --> comment leaves out the rest of its section, up to the next heading of the same or a higher level. Transitions between docs are ordinary scenes, for example a hidden run: cd other && clear and a scene with an overlay.

docs.title: Heading overlays
docs.text:
heading_overlays: N shows the headings down to level N, each level in its own built-in style: heading-1 is a title card in the centre, deeper levels appear at the top right and fade after a few seconds. {levels: N, breadcrumb: true} shows levels 2 to N as one overlay instead, Environments › Compose › Services, which stays while its section plays. Long breadcrumbs shorten their middle parts to … first (max_length, default 50); separator changes the ›.

Style position size bold duration_ms heading-1 center large yes 2.5s; while the doc's intro is spoken, until it ends (since 0.7) heading-2 top-right large yes 3s heading-3 top-right medium no 3s heading-4 and deeper top-right small no 2.5s breadcrumb top-right small no until the section ends file top small no until the scene ends

The title card stays while the text before the first block is spoken, so the intro does not play over an empty prompt; a duration_ms for heading-1 in overlay_styles applies instead. Change them like any style in overlay_styles.

docs.title: Snippets and mkdocs
docs.text:
The doc is read the way this repo's mkdocs config renders it: admonitions, collapsible blocks and content tabs (pymdownx.tabbed) as described on this page, and --8<-- "path" snippets (with an optional :start:end line range) inserted before reading, relative to the snippets base_path in the nearest mkdocs.yml, else the repository root. Errors in an inserted snippet name the snippet file and line. Headings with an id (## Title {#custom}) are selected by that id.

Block snippets (--8<-- on a line of its own), URL snippets and named snippet sections are not supported and are reported as errors.

docs.title: Checking the result
docs.text:
narratty validate reports problems at the Markdown file and line. Since 0.7 it also warns, on stderr and without failing, about what expands fine but is likely not what the author meant:

Warning Fix No command runs in the video Label command blocks console (with $ prompts), bash or sh A left-out block has $ lines Label it console, or mark it narratty="show" Code blocks in a language such as python or yaml are left out (one warning for all) Mark one narratty="show" to show it, give it a title to write it to that file, or skip it A table is left out A table or slide comment, or skip to leave it out on purpose Output shown looks like an error (error:, Error: …, ERROR …, fatal:, a Python traceback) Mark the block expect-failure if the command is meant to fail A command ends in & without redirecting its output Its late output lands in later commands; write cmd > server.log 2>&1 & A focus ID is not in the diagram (flowcharts and sequence diagrams) Use an ID from the source; the warning suggests the closest, and a participant's id for its as label Narration says "above", "below", "click here" or "the following command" (each one) Reword it so it works when heard, such as "next" or "this command"; "below it" and "above the line" are fine

lint: false on the entry, or in the doc's spec comment, turns the warnings off. narratty plan --sources SPEC lists every scene with the Markdown line it comes from, and what was left out and why. narratty compile SPEC prints the spec with every markdown entry replaced by its scenes: a way out of Markdown input, or a frozen copy to build from.

Sandboxed runs only mount the spec file into the container, so they get the expanded spec; the Markdown docs stay on the host.

docs.title: Checking docs in CI
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

narratty check runs the doc's commands the way the video would, without recording, voice or end card. It fails when a command fails (exit code 7) or prints something else than the doc shows (exit code 8), with a diff:

narratty check docs/install.md

In a console block, the lines after a $ command, up to the next one, are what it prints:

$ echo "Hello from Markdown"
Hello from Markdown
  • Colours, trailing spaces and blank lines at the start and end do not count.
  • A line ... stands for any lines, also none; ... within a line for any text, as in Python 3....
  • A command without output lines in the doc runs, but its output is not compared.
  • narratty="any-output" on a block, or check_output: false on the entry, turns the comparison off.
  • Builds check exit codes, but do not compare output.
  • The summary counts no-run commands apart, as shown only. When no command ran, check warns, since it checked nothing (since 0.7).

The comparison is the run action's expect_output, which narratty compile shows. narratty compile SPEC --fingerprint tells when a committed video is older than its doc.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
narratty completes commands, options and option values in bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell.

narratty --install-completion      # detects your shell and installs the script
narratty --show-completion zsh     # print the script, e.g. for your dotfiles

Restart your shell afterwards. Completion never loads voice models or starts containers, so it stays fast; CI enforces a cold-start budget for it.

docs.title: Spec reference
docs.text: A narratty video is described by a .narratty.yaml file. For a video made from a doc, it is mostly a markdown entry plus the voice and the look, and a doc can also be built on its own with no YAML file at all (Building a doc on its own). narratty init writes a commented starter, narratty validate checks one, and narratty schema prints the JSON Schema.

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text:
The first line narratty init writes tells your editor where the schema is:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ditschi/narratty/v0.2.0/schema/v1.json

Editors that use yaml-language-server read that comment and then offer completion, hover docs and inline errors for the spec: VS Code with the Red Hat YAML extension, Neovim or Helix with yaml-language-server, and JetBrains IDEs. The schema is committed to the repository as schema/v1.json, so each release tag serves the schema of that release. init points the line at the tag of the narratty version you have installed; development builds point at main.

Offline, or to pin a local copy, write the schema to a file and reference it relatively:

narratty schema > .narratty.schema.json

# yaml-language-server: $schema=./.narratty.schema.json

Unknown keys are errors, and validate reports every problem with its line and column, plus a "did you mean" for typos:

$ narratty validate demo.narratty.yaml
error: demo.narratty.yaml: 1 problem
  demo.narratty.yaml:4:9: scenes[0].actions[0]: unknown action 'type_comand' (did you mean 'type_command'?)
hint: Run `narratty schema` for the full list of keys.

Valid lines that can be left out or written shorter are reported as hints; they do not fail validation:

$ narratty validate demo.narratty.yaml
hint: demo.narratty.yaml:3:3: tts.voice: same as the default; leave it out
hint: demo.narratty.yaml:12:9: scenes[1].actions[0]: 'hold: auto' has no effect at the end of a scene; leave it out
ok demo.narratty.yaml: 2 scenes, 2 narrated, voice kokoro/af_heart

docs.title: Durations
docs.text: Every *_ms key and hold take milliseconds (1500) or a duration with a unit: 800ms, 1.5s, 2m.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Key Default Meaning version 1 Spec format version meta.title Untitled Title of the video tts Voice settings, see below timing Sync settings, see below terminal Look of the recorded terminal requires.tools [] Extra commands the demo needs (checked by doctor) requires.narratty unset narratty versions the spec needs, e.g. ">=0.3"; see Spec versions (since 0.5) workspace What directory the demo runs in sandbox Permissions of the container environment Run the demo shell in a project image, Compose service or container (since 0.3) end_card on Closing card, see below subtitles none none, files, track or burn; see Subtitles (since 0.3) overlay_styles {} Named overlay styles; see Overlays (since 0.3) narration all Default narration rule of markdown entries: all or none; see Markdown input (since 0.5) slides.theme dark Look of every slide: dark or light (since 0.6) scenes required At least one scene, or a markdown entry

Directory the demo runs in, relative to the spec mode snapshot snapshot (throwaway copy), rw (the real directory) or ro (read-only) include_uncommitted true Copy uncommitted files into the snapshot caches {} Caches kept across runs, name: /path/in/container artifacts [] Paths copied out of the workspace after the run

docs.text:
Since narratty 0.3.

Runs the demo shell in your project's image, Compose service or container; see Project environments.

Set exactly one of image, compose and container.

docs.title: end_card
docs.text:
The video ends with a short card that shows the narratty logo above "Created with narratty", a link to this documentation and a QR code of the link. The QR code sits beside the logo and text, or above the text on a narrow terminal. When space runs out, the logo goes first, then the QR code. The QR code is drawn in black and white so it scans on any theme.

Key Default Meaning enabled unset true or false; unset follows your config (on by default) duration_ms 4000 How long the card stays on screen (at least 1000) qr true Show the QR code

end_card: false is short for end_card: {enabled: false}. To turn the card off for every video, put this in ~/.config/narratty/config.toml:

[end_card]
enabled = false

--end-card / --no-end-card on the command line win over the spec, and the spec wins over the config.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning id required Lowercase letters, digits, - and _; unique narration none Text spoken while the scene plays actions [] What happens in the terminal hidden false Run without recording (setup); cannot have narration typing_speed_ms terminal's Per-scene typing speed pause_ms timing.pause_ms Per-scene pause after each key and ctrl_sequence (since 0.3) narration_start with_actions Or after_actions timelapse none Show the scene this many times faster (greater than 1) (since 0.3) expect_exit success Exit codes of the scene's commands: success, failure or any; see Exit codes (since 0.3) fast --fast true/false: fill long pauses with still frames or not; see Fast pauses (since 0.3)

A scene lasts as long as its actions or its narration plus narration_buffer_ms, whichever is longer.

A scenes item can instead be a markdown entry, - markdown: docs/guide.md, which turns the doc's paragraphs and code blocks into scenes where it stands; see Markdown input (since 0.5).

docs.title: Timelapse
docs.text:
A long step (a download, a build) can be shown sped up instead of hidden:

- id: install
  narration: Installing the dependencies takes a while; here it is eight times faster.
  actions:
    - run: npm ci
- id: install-runs
  timelapse: 8
  actions:
    - wait: {screen: "added \\d+ packages", timeout_ms: 600000}
  • The whole scene is sped up, typing included, so type the command in the scene before and only wait in the timelapse scene.
  • Narration plays at normal speed. If it is longer than the sped-up footage, the last frame stays until it ends. With narration_start: after_actions it starts when the footage ends.
  • A timelapse scene cannot be hidden or use hold: auto.
  • narratty plan cannot know how long the waits take, so its length for the scene counts only the fixed actions.
  • The video is re-encoded once (H.264) to speed up the scenes. narratty tape shows where the scenes are, but plain vhs does not speed them up.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Action Example Does run - run: ls -la Types the command, presses Enter, pauses timing.run_hold_ms; may set its own expect_exit (since 0.3) and expect_output (since 0.6, see Expected output), show and max_lines (since 0.7, see Shown commands) type_command - type_command: "ls -la" Types the text, without Enter ctrl_sequence - ctrl_sequence: C-c Presses Ctrl plus a key key - key: Enter or - key: Down 3 Presses a key, optionally repeated hold - hold: 1.5s or - hold: auto Waits; auto waits until the narration is done wait - wait: "Done" or - wait: {screen: "Done", timeout_ms: 1m} Waits until the screen matches a regex (default timeout 15 s) wait - wait: {prompt: true, timeout_ms: 10m} Waits until the command has finished and the prompt is back (since 0.3) diff - diff or - diff: [src, README.md] Shows what changed since the recording started, optionally only for some paths (since 0.3) focus - focus: explorer Moves the keyboard to explorer or terminal (editor layout) (since 0.3) reveal - reveal: src/app.py Selects a path, relative to the workspace, in the explorer (editor layout) (since 0.3) overlay - overlay: "Open src/main.py" Shows text over the video; see Overlays (since 0.3) browser - browser: docs/site/index.html Shows a web page over the terminal; see Browser views (since 0.3) slide - slide: {mermaid: "flowchart LR\n a --> b"} Shows a table, diagram, image or HTML page full screen; see Slides (since 0.6)

Keys: Enter, Tab, Space, Backspace, Delete, Escape, Up, Down, Left, Right, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, Insert. Names are case-insensitive. Older specs write Enter as - enter; it still works, key: Enter is the current form.

Every list item starts with -. A scene always waits for its narration after its last action, so hold: auto is only needed in the middle of a scene; a scene has at most one. See Writing specs for when to use which action.

diff, focus and reveal take no time in the video: they run while recording is hidden, and the screen changes at once. Add a hold after them for a pause.

diff compares against a copy of the workspace taken when the recording starts, kept outside the workspace (its own .git is not touched). It honours .gitignore and leaves out __pycache__. The output is coloured with delta, else bat, else git. In the plain layout the screen is cleared and the diff is printed; in the editor layout it opens in a popup that stays until the next key press of the scene or its end.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
narratty logs the exit code of every command line run at the shell prompt and checks it against expect_exit after recording:

Value Build fails when success (default) a command exits non-zero failure no command exits non-zero, e.g. an error demo that suddenly works any never; exit codes are not checked 
- id: typo
  narration: A typo gives a helpful error.
  expect_exit: failure
  actions:
    - run: git stauts
- id: retry
  actions:
    - run: make test
    - run: curl https://example.org
      expect_exit: any            # this command only

The most specific setting wins: a run action's expect_exit, then the scene's, then the command line (--ignore-exit makes any the default), then success.

The build exits with code 7 and names each offending command; the video is still written so you can inspect it. A line's exit code is that of its last command (a; b reports b). Commands stopped with C-c or C-z do not count as failures. Commands inside programs (a REPL, an editor, a nested shell) are not checked, nor is anything with shell: sh. In the editor layout, the terminal pane's commands are checked. In a project environment the log is read from its container after recording. With bash 3.2 (macOS's default) narratty turns on shell history to read the command lines, so key: Up recalls earlier commands there.

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

A run action's expect_output is what the command prints. narratty check runs the commands without recording a video and compares; builds do not.

- id: version
  actions:
    - run: python --version
      expect_output: Python 3...
    - wait: {prompt: true}
  • The output is compared as plain text: colours and other escape sequences are left out, a carriage return redraws its line, trailing spaces and blank lines at the start and end do not count.
  • A line ... stands for any number of lines, also none; ... within a line for any text there.
  • The output ends where the prompt is back, so follow the command with wait: {prompt: true}. Markdown input does that and fills in expect_output from the output a console block shows.
  • Output without a final newline (printf '{"a":1}', curl -s) is fine: the prompt then follows it on the same line, and the wait still sees it. Late output from a background job can push the prompt off its line; check notices that the shell is idle, but a build waits until the timeout, so redirect such a job's output (server > server.log &).
  • Output is not compared in the editor layout, where tmux redraws it.

narratty check exits with code 8 and shows a diff for each command that printed something else.

docs.title: Shown commands
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.7.

A run action can show something else than it runs. show is the command typed on screen; run runs in its place, and the video shows its output. max_lines cuts the output after that many lines and ends it with ... (N more lines).

- id: install
  narration: Install the package.
  actions:
    - run: pip install -e .          # what the video can run
      show: pip install tally        # what readers type
    - wait: {prompt: true}
- id: tests
  actions:
    - run: pytest -v
      max_lines: 10
    - wait: {prompt: true}
  • The shown command is typed at the scene's speed. After Enter, unrecorded, the line is replaced by run and redrawn as the shown command, so no ^C or second command appears. run must be a single line; show may have several.
  • With max_lines, the command's output (stdout and stderr) goes through awk. The command no longer writes to a terminal, so programs that colour their output only for terminals print it plain. The exit code stays the command's (in bash, zsh and fish).
  • Exit codes are checked as usual, those of run.
  • narratty check runs run as it is: without show, and without cutting the output, so expect_output is compared with all of it.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.3.

An overlay shows text over the video, in a rounded, semi-transparent box: a chapter title, the file the narration talks about. It stays readable while the terminal scrolls.

overlay_styles:
  file: {position: top, size: small, color: "#f1fa8c"}

scenes:
  - id: setup
    narration: Let's set up the project.
    actions:
      - overlay: {text: "1 · Setup", style: chapter}
      - run: make setup
      - overlay: Run the tests next
      - overlay: {text: src/greet/__main__.py, style: file, duration_ms: 3000}

The overlay appears where its action stands in the scene. It stays until the first of: duration_ms has passed, another overlay takes its position, or the scene ends. With keep: true it stays past the scene until another overlay takes its position. The same overlay (text and style) in consecutive scenes shows as one, without fading in again (since 0.5). The box is sized around the text; \n starts a new line. The top right is usually free of terminal text; the bottom is shared with burned-in subtitles.

overlay: "text" uses the default style. A mapping takes text, an optional style and any style key to change just this overlay:

Style key default Meaning position bottom-right top-left, top, top-right, left, center, right, bottom-left, bottom, bottom-right size medium small, medium, large, or a factor of terminal.font_size (1.3 = medium) color #ffffff Text colour, #rrggbb background #000000b3 Box colour, #rrggbbaa (the last two digits are the opacity) box true false shows the text alone, with a dark outline bold false Bold text duration_ms unset Hide after this long keep false Stay past the end of the scene

Built-in styles: default (above) and chapter (top-right, large, bold, hides after 3s). Since 0.5 a chapter no longer keeps; overlay_styles: {chapter: {keep: true}} brings back the old behaviour. Markdown input adds heading-1 to heading-4, breadcrumb and file (since 0.5). overlay_styles changes them or adds your own; each style starts from default, so it only lists what differs. Overlays fade in and out. They need the mp4 to be re-encoded, which build does when a spec has any; in the cast page they are drawn over the player and follow its clock.

docs.title: Browser views
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.3.

A browser view shows a web page or a local HTML file as a browser renders it, for example the rendered documentation next to its Markdown source. Chromium (which VHS records with) captures the page at the video's width; the view covers the terminal under an address bar until its scene ends.

sandbox:
  network: full       # only for web pages; local files need no network
scenes:
  - id: page
    narration: This is the page you should see.
    actions:
      - browser: {url: "https://github.com/ditschi/narratty", scroll: 1400}
  - id: docs
    narration: The built documentation looks like this.
    actions:
      - run: mkdocs build
      - wait: "Documentation built"
      - browser: {url: site/index.html, scroll: auto}
Key Default Meaning url required An http(s) URL, an HTML file in the workspace, or a data: URL (since 0.5) address the URL Text in the address bar (since 0.5) scroll none auto scrolls to the end of the page (at most 4 screens), a number scrolls that many pixels duration_ms unset Hide after this long load_ms 5000 How long the page may load before it is captured

browser: URL is short for browser: {url: URL}. The page is captured once, after it has loaded; scrolling pauses a moment at the top and at the bottom and takes the rest of the time the view is shown. A later view in the same scene replaces an earlier one, and overlays are drawn on top. Web pages need network access: in the container that is sandbox: {network: full}. Prefer local files for pages behind a login; narratty never signs in. The whole example is in examples/browser.

Since 0.6, Mermaid diagrams on a page are drawn before the capture: elements with the class mermaid (<pre class="mermaid">flowchart LR …</pre>) on a page that does not load Mermaid itself. The narratty image brings mermaid.min.js, so this works without network; native renders read it from NARRATTY_MERMAID_JS or the data directory (narratty doctor shows where).

docs.title: Slides
docs.text:
Since narratty 0.6.

A slide shows one table, Mermaid diagram, image, HTML page or piece of code full screen over the terminal, with an optional title, while the narration talks about it. Like a browser view it stays until its scene ends or duration_ms has passed, and a later slide or browser view in the same scene replaces it.

slides: {theme: dark}              # the default; light is the other look
scenes:
  - id: risks
    narration: Pinch points are the highest risk. Keep the guard closed.
    actions:
      - slide:
          title: Safety risks
          table:
            header: [Hazard, Severity, Mitigation]
            rows:
              - [Pinch point, high, Keep the guard closed]
              - [Hot surface, medium, Wear `gloves`]
          highlight: 1
  - id: flow
    narration: A spec becomes a video in three steps.
    actions:
      - slide: {title: Build flow, mermaid: "flowchart LR\n  spec --> plan --> build --> mp4"}
  - id: screenshot
    narration: This is the result.
    actions:
      - slide: {image: docs/assets/overlays.png, theme: light}
Key Meaning table {header: [...], rows: [[...], ...]}, the list of rows, each with as many cells as the header; cells are inline Markdown (`code`, **bold**, links) mermaid The source of a Mermaid diagram, drawn without network focus Mermaid node or subgraph ID to emphasize during narration (since 0.7) image A PNG, JPEG, GIF, SVG or WebP file in the workspace, or a data: URL html An HTML file in the workspace or a data: URL, shown as it is (no title or theme) code Source code, syntax-highlighted and sized to fit (since 0.7) lang Language of code, such as json or yaml (any Pygments name); unset or unknown: plain text (since 0.7) title Text above the content highlight Table row to highlight, from 1 rows Table rows per page, a number (not the rows list inside table); the page with the highlighted row is shown, with a page counter page Table page to show when no row is highlighted theme dark or light; defaults to slides.theme duration_ms Hide after this long

For a diagram walkthrough, repeat the same source in successive scenes and change focus; each highlight stays in place for that scene's narration. focus is the ID from the diagram source (api, api-gateway, a subgraph's ID) and must name exactly one node or subgraph, or in a sequence diagram a participant (C for participant C as Client); otherwise the render fails and lists the IDs it found:

scenes:
  - id: api
    narration: Requests enter through the API.
    actions:
      - slide:
          mermaid: |
            flowchart LR
              api --> db
          focus: api
  - id: database
    narration: The API stores each request in the database.
    actions:
      - slide:
          mermaid: |
            flowchart LR
              api --> db
          focus: db

Exactly one of table, mermaid, image, html and code is given. A table taller than the slide moves up so that the highlighted row stays in view. A Markdown doc makes slides from its tables, mermaid blocks, images and blocks marked show; see Markdown input.

docs.title: Spec versions
docs.text:
version changes only when a spec that worked before would break: a key is removed, renamed or changes its meaning. New keys, actions and short forms keep the version, so every version: 1 spec keeps working with newer narratty releases.

A spec that uses newer keys needs a newer narratty, which version does not tell. requires.narratty does:

requires:
  narratty: ">=0.3"   # uses run, key: Enter and durations

narratty checks it before anything else in the spec, so an older narratty that knows the key reports the version to install instead of the keys it does not know. Releases before 0.5 do not know requires.narratty and reject it as an unknown key.

Release Added to version: 1 0.3 run action, key: Enter (the bare - enter still works), durations like 1.5s, wait: "pattern", wait: {prompt: true}, timing.run_hold_ms, timing.pause_ms and scene pause_ms, tts.lexicon, subtitles, environment, sandbox.docker, terminal.layout, overlays (overlay, overlay_styles), browser, diff, focus, reveal, scene timelapse, expect_exit and fast 0.5 requires.narratty, markdown scene entries and the top-level narration (Markdown input), overlay styles heading-1 to heading-4, breadcrumb and file, browser address and data: URLs 0.6 slide action and slides.theme, Mermaid diagrams in browser views, run expect_output; in Markdown input the table, slide, pause and spec comments, mermaid blocks, check_output and the any-output block option 0.7 slide focus, code and lang, run show and max_lines; in Markdown input the focus, skip-rest, run and clear comments, the slide comment's focus and hold keys, the table comment's hold and a list for its say, the show block option and the say=…, instead=…, lines=…, until=…, then=… and timeout=… block options, sections with include / exclude, and the entry keys footnotes, admonitions, image_titles, lint, say and clear_on

docs.title: Demo toolkit
docs.text:
The toolkit is a set of statically linked command-line tools that look good in recordings, plus settings tuned for video. It runs in any Linux image (Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine, UBI, even busybox), as any user, without a package manager.

Tool Use in demos bat Show files with syntax highlighting delta Show diffs with syntax highlighting (used by the diff action) eza ls and eza --tree with colours and icons fd, rg Find files and text jq Pretty-print JSON micro Editor with familiar keys (Ctrl+s saves, Ctrl+q quits) yazi File explorer with a preview file File type detection (yazi needs it for previews) tmux Split the terminal into panes zsh Alternative shell (terminal.shell: zsh)

It also brings the Symbols Nerd Font (icons in yazi and eza --icons), a tmux.conf with a quiet status line and titled panes, and configs for yazi, bat and micro. Licenses are in /usr/local/share/narratty/licenses.

docs.title: In the narratty image
docs.text: The narratty image contains the toolkit, with its settings active. Specs that run in the container can use all tools directly.

docs.title: In your own image
docs.text:
The toolkit is published as ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit, an image that holds only these files. Add it to a Dockerfile with one line:

COPY --from=ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit:latest / /usr/local/
ENV YAZI_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/yazi \
    BAT_CONFIG_PATH=/usr/local/share/narratty/bat/config \
    MICRO_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/micro
  • The target must be /usr/local: zsh and tmux look for their files there.
  • COPY needs no USER root, and nothing is installed at run time.
  • Instead of the ENV lines, a shell can load the settings with . /usr/local/share/narratty/env.sh. tmux reads its settings from /usr/local/etc/tmux.conf on its own; a ~/.tmux.conf still wins.
  • Images exist for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Tags follow narratty's versions (<version>, <major.minor>, latest, edge); pin a version for reproducible builds.

docs.title: In a dev container
docs.text:
The toolkit goes into the image the dev container is built from. Pick the case that matches your setup.

devcontainer.json with a Dockerfile. Add the lines to that Dockerfile. In a multi-stage Dockerfile, add them to the stage the dev container uses (build.target):

# .devcontainer/Dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:3.12
# ... your setup ...
COPY --from=ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit:latest / /usr/local/
ENV YAZI_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/yazi \
    BAT_CONFIG_PATH=/usr/local/share/narratty/bat/config \
    MICRO_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/micro

devcontainer.json with only image. Replace image with a build of a two-line Dockerfile:

// .devcontainer/devcontainer.json
{
  "build": { "dockerfile": "Dockerfile" }   // was: "image": "ghcr.io/acme/dev:2"
}

# .devcontainer/Dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/acme/dev:2
COPY --from=ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit:latest / /usr/local/
ENV YAZI_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/yazi \
    BAT_CONFIG_PATH=/usr/local/share/narratty/bat/config \
    MICRO_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/micro

Docker Compose, without touching the project. An override file adds the toolkit on top of the service's image with an inline Dockerfile (Compose 2.17 or later):

# compose.narratty.yaml
services:
  dev:
    image: acme-dev:narratty          # own tag, the original image stays as it is
    build: !override                  # replaces the service's own build settings
      dockerfile_inline: |
        FROM ghcr.io/acme/dev:2
        COPY --from=ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit:latest / /usr/local/
        ENV YAZI_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/yazi \
            BAT_CONFIG_PATH=/usr/local/share/narratty/bat/config \
            MICRO_CONFIG_HOME=/usr/local/share/narratty/micro

docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.narratty.yaml up -d --build
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.narratty.yaml exec dev bash

If the service is built from its own Dockerfile (build: in compose.yaml), build it first without the override and use its image name after FROM:

docker compose build dev
docker compose config --images      # the image name to put after FROM

The dev container keeps its user; nothing runs as root at run time.

docs.title: Onboarding videos
docs.text:
To run the whole demo in the project's image, Compose service or dev container, use a project environment; the toolkit is mounted there automatically. The pattern below records the steps that lead into the container.

A video that clones a repository, starts its dev container and works inside it needs Docker during the recording. Either give the sandboxed demo your engine with sandbox.docker: true (full host access, you approve it once), or run with --runtime native:

sandbox:
  docker: true
  network: allowlist                   # for git clone
  allow_hosts: [github.com:443]
scenes:
  - id: clone
    narration: Clone the repository.
    actions:
      - run: git clone https://github.com/acme/app && cd app
      - wait: {screen: "done\\.", timeout_ms: 120000}
  - id: toolkit                  # add the toolkit, unrecorded
    hidden: true
    actions:
      - run: >-
          echo 'COPY --from=ghcr.io/ditschi/narratty-toolkit:latest / /usr/local/'
          >> .devcontainer/Dockerfile
  - id: build
    narration: Build and start the dev container. This is sped up.
    actions:
      - run: docker compose up -d --build && echo rea""dy
  - id: build-runs               # the build output, ten times faster
    timelapse: 10
    actions:
      - wait: {screen: "\\nready", timeout_ms: 900000}
  - id: enter
    narration: Open a shell in the dev container.
    actions:
      - run: docker compose exec dev bash
  - id: settings
    hidden: true
    actions:
      - run: . /usr/local/share/narratty/env.sh
  - id: explore
    narration: This is the project inside the container.
    actions:
      - run: eza --tree --level 2

Things to watch:

  • A timelapse scene shows the build sped up. To leave it out instead, make the scene hidden: true: hidden scenes take no time in the video, and the screen is cleared after them.
  • echo rea""dy prints ready, but the typed command does not match the wait.
  • Instead of editing the Dockerfile, the hidden scene can write the Compose override and start with both files.
  • The appended COPY line lands in the last stage of the Dockerfile. If the dev container builds an earlier stage (target:), add it there.
  • Viewers who follow the video do not have that line. Use the toolkit to show the project, not for steps they are meant to repeat.
  • The dev container keeps running after the render. End with a hidden scene that leaves it (exit) and runs docker compose down.

docs.title: Editor layout
docs.text:
terminal.layout: editor records a layout like an editor: yazi as explorer and preview on top, the shell below, in a tmux window of its own. narratty builds it before the first scene and closes it before the end card; the spec only describes the demo:

terminal:
  layout: editor
scenes:
  - id: explore
    narration: Open the source folder in the explorer.
    actions:
      - focus: explorer        # keys now go to yazi
      - key: Right
  - id: tests
    narration: Reveal jumps to a file, and Enter opens it in micro.
    actions:
      - reveal: tests/test_greet.py
      - key: Enter
  - id: diff
    narration: The diff shows what the demo changed.
    actions:
      - diff
  • The shell starts with focus. focus: explorer and focus: terminal switch.
  • In the explorer, the arrow keys move and Enter opens a file in $EDITOR; the layout sets it to micro when that is installed and EDITOR is unset.
  • reveal selects a path relative to the workspace, whichever pane has focus.
  • diff opens a popup over the layout; the next key press of the scene, or its end, closes it.
  • After a hidden scene the shell pane is cleared.
  • The layout needs tmux and yazi, diff needs git; the narratty image has all three. It runs its own tmux server with its own settings, so a ~/.tmux.conf does not change the recording.
  • Both also work with an environment.

The editor layout example shows all of it.

docs.title: Voices and audio cache
docs.text:
narratty speaks with local text-to-speech engines; nothing is sent to a cloud service.

Provider Sound Languages Download kokoro (default) natural English (US, UK), Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Hindi, Japanese, Chinese one 205 MB model shared by all voices (af_heart, bf_emma, …) piper clear, more synthetic many, including German about 60 MB per voice (en_US-lessac-medium, de_DE-thorsten-medium, …)

Both come with narratty. Without a tts block a spec uses Kokoro with af_heart; with only provider, the voice defaults to that provider's first voice:

tts:
  provider: piper
  voice: de_DE-thorsten-medium
  piper:
    length_scale: 1.1

narratty uses Kokoro's fp16 model: half the size of the full model, faster on a CPU and sounds the same.

docs.title: Listing and downloading voices
docs.text:
narratty voices                      # curated voices of both providers
narratty voices --provider piper --installed
narratty voices pull bf_emma

narratty tts and narratty build download a missing voice on first use; pass --offline (or set NARRATTY_OFFLINE=1) to fail instead. Kokoro model files are checked against pinned SHA-256 sums.

Voices live in the data directory, ~/.local/share/narratty on Linux (override with NARRATTY_DATA_DIR). To use a Piper voice that is not in the curated list, copy its <id>.onnx and <id>.onnx.json into <data dir>/piper/ and set tts.voice: <id>.

docs.title: Synthesizing narration
docs.text:
narratty tts demo.narratty.yaml

prints one row per narrated scene with the clip's length and whether it came from the cache.

Speed on 4 CPU cores: Kokoro needs about 0.2 s per second of speech, Piper less but loads the voice for every clip, so Piper synthesizes up to 4 clips at once. Kokoro's int8 model is about five times slower on CPU than the default fp16. While editing, build --draft skips TTS completely.

docs.title: Pronunciation
docs.text:
Write narration with the real spelling of technical terms (.bazelrc, kubectl, bm_rat_b), not a phonetic workaround such as "dot Basel R C". The text stays searchable and correct in the spec. The engines already say most terms well (bazel, YAML, bm_rat_b), and narratty speaks a leading dot as "dot". For the rest, the lexicon tells the engine how to say a term:

tts:
  lexicon:
    k8s: "kubernetes"
    kubectl: "cube C T L"

Entries come from four levels; a later level overrides an earlier one:

Level Where Built-in shipped with narratty (kubectl, stdout, CLI, …); English voices only User ~/.config/narratty/lexicon.toml Project nearest narratty.lexicon.toml from the spec's directory up to the git root Spec tts.lexicon

The TOML files use the same pairs:

kubectl = "cube C T L"
[k8s]
say = "kubernetes"
  • Matching is whole-word. A term with a capital letter matches only that case (API); an all-lowercase term matches any case (k8s, K8s).
  • A leading dot is spoken as "dot", also before a term with an entry: .kubectl becomes "dot cube C T L".
  • Only the spoken text changes; the lexicon result is part of the audio cache key.
  • Sandboxed runs get the user and project entries from the host.
narratty lexicon show demo.narratty.yaml    # merged entries and their source
narratty lexicon check demo.narratty.yaml   # dotted, snake_case, camelCase, ALL-CAPS or digit words without an entry

When an AI writes the scene list, tell it to spell terms as written in the code and to put pronunciations in tts.lexicon; then run narratty lexicon check and listen to narratty tts.

docs.title: Audio cache
docs.text:
Every clip is stored under a key made of the provider, voice, spoken text, model version and provider options, so only changed narration is synthesized again. The cache is in ~/.cache/narratty on Linux (override with NARRATTY_CACHE_DIR).

narratty cache info
narratty cache prune --older-than 30d     # clips not used for 30 days
narratty cache prune --all

docs.title: Licences
docs.text: Piper (piper-tts) is GPL-3.0; narratty only runs it as a separate process, so narratty itself stays MIT. Each Piper voice has its own licence, linked from its model card (see narratty voices and the piper-voices repository). The Kokoro model is Apache-2.0.

docs.title: Writing specs
docs.text:
A Markdown doc can be built on its own, or a spec points at it and sets the voice and the look. Write scenes in YAML for what a doc doesn't hold: an intro or outro, a transition between docs, hidden setup, or a demo with no doc behind it. This page is about those scenes.

A good spec reads like a script: narration and the commands, nothing else. The defaults cover the common case, so write only what differs from them.

docs.title: Leave out the defaults
docs.text:
Every key has a default (see the spec reference). This is a complete spec:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ditschi/narratty/main/schema/v1.json
scenes:
  - id: intro
    narration: This is a quick tour of the repository layout.
    actions:
      - run: ls -la

Repeating defaults such as tts: {provider: kokoro, voice: af_heart} or the terminal size only makes the spec longer and hides the settings that matter.

docs.title: Scenes wait for their narration
docs.text:
A scene lasts until its actions are done and its narration has finished, plus timing.narration_buffer_ms. The pause that fills the gap goes after the last action. So:

  • A scene that only talks needs no actions.
  • hold: auto at the end of a scene does nothing extra. Use it only in the middle of a scene, when the actions after it should wait for the narration.
# not needed
- id: intro
  narration: This demo looks like an editor.
  actions:
    - hold: auto

# enough
- id: intro
  narration: This demo looks like an editor.

# hold: auto in the middle: show the result while talking, then clear the screen
- id: result
  narration: The build is green, all tests passed.
  actions:
    - run: make test
    - wait: passed
    - hold: auto
    - ctrl_sequence: C-l

docs.title: run for commands, type_command for typing
docs.text:
run types a command, presses Enter and pauses for timing.run_hold_ms (500 ms), so the viewer sees the output before the next command is typed.

# long form
- type_command: git status
- key: Enter
- hold: 500ms

# same thing
- run: git status

Use type_command for input that is not a finished command: text in an editor, a prompt that is answered later, or a command that is edited before Enter:

- type_command: git commit -m "wip"
- hold: 1s                   # let the viewer read it
- key: Backspace 4           # remove wip"
- type_command: fix"
- key: Enter

Change the pause for every run in the spec with timing.run_hold_ms. For a single longer pause, add a hold after that run.

docs.title: Wait for output instead of guessing
docs.text:
A command that takes a moment should be followed by wait, not by a long hold. The video then continues as soon as the output is there:

- run: docker compose up -d
- wait: Started

wait: "pattern" uses the default timeout of 15 seconds. Give the mapping form only for a different timeout:

- wait: {screen: "Successfully built", timeout_ms: 5m}

Slow setup (installs, builds, downloads) belongs in a hidden: true scene, which is run but not recorded.

docs.title: Only divergent values per scene
docs.text:
Set a value once at the top and override it only where a scene differs:

terminal:
  typing_speed_ms: 30          # the whole video types a bit faster

scenes:
  - id: long-command
    typing_speed_ms: 10        # this one command would take too long otherwise
    actions:
      - run: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/acme/tool:latest check

The same goes for pauses. Every key and ctrl_sequence is followed by timing.pause_ms (100 ms). A scene that steps through a menu sets its own pause instead of a hold after every key:

# instead of a hold after every key
- id: explore
  pause_ms: 600ms
  actions:
    - key: Right
    - key: Right
    - key: Down

docs.title: YAML pitfalls
docs.text:
• List items start with -. * item is Markdown, not YAML (* starts an alias), and fails to parse.
  • Quote text that contains :, # or starts with a special character (*, &, !, %, @, `, {, [).
  • >- folds a long command over several lines; a line break becomes a space.
  • Comments (#) inside a > or | block are part of the text.

docs.title: Let validate find redundant lines
docs.text:
narratty validate reports every problem with its line and column. With the schema line at the top, editors show the same problems while you type. Lines that are valid but redundant are reported as hints:

  • values equal to their default
  • hold: auto at the end of a scene, or with narration_start: after_actions
  • type_command directly followed by Enter (write run)
  • wait: {screen: ...} without a timeout (write wait: "...")
  • the bare - enter (write key: Enter)

docs.title: Say which narratty a spec needs
docs.text:
A spec shared with others should name the oldest narratty it works with. Keys added in a release are marked "(since X.Y)" in the spec reference:

requires:
  narratty: ">=0.3"

docs.title: Specs written by an AI agent
docs.text: Point the agent at this page and let it run narratty validate after each change until it reports no problems and no hints.
